_meta.APPLICABILITY_WARNING: VB-1180 covers PA-28-161 serials 28-8316001 and up. N84054 is serial 28-8116257, which falls in FAA TCDS 2A13 item XVI-A (28-7716001 through 28-8216300) and is covered by Piper Report VB-880. VB-1180 is therefore the RIGHT MODEL but the WRONG REVISION for this tail number. Section 7 systems descriptions are the same airframe and carry across. Weights, anything that scales with weight, and the Section 5 performance charts DO NOT. Every leaf below carries a carries_to_1981 flag. See serial_caveats.
_meta.engine_dash_number_warning: TCDS 2A13 and POH 1.3/2.7 both approve EITHER the O-320-D2A or the O-320-D3G. The FAA registry records N84054's engine only as '0-320 SERIES'. The installed dash number must be read off the engine data plate; do not assert one in the oral.

general_statement.value: This airplane must be operated as a normal or utility category airplane in compliance with the operating limitations stated in the form of placards and markings and those given in this section and handbook.

yellow_arc_caution_smooth_air_only.note: POH 2.5 'Yellow Arc (Caution Range - Smooth Air Only) 126 to 160'.

green_arc_normal_operating.note: POH 2.5 'Green Arc (Normal Operating Range) 50 to 126'. The bottom end is VS1 at 2440 lb, so the arc start is weight-dependent; the markings on HIS instrument are whatever VB-880 specifies.

white_arc_flap_down.note: POH 2.5 'White Arc (Flap Down) 44 to 103'. Bottom end is VSO at 2440 lb; top end is VFE.

blue_line.note: There is no blue radial line on this airplane. VB-1180 2.5 lists exactly four markings - one red radial, one yellow arc, one green arc, one white arc. Blue radial = single-engine best rate of climb on a twin; not applicable.

engine_model.note: POH 2.7(c) and 1.3(c) print both, exactly as the TCDS approves both. The installed dash number must come from the engine data plate.

maximum_horsepower.note: POH 2.7(d)(1) 'Maximum Horsepower 160'. Also 1.3(d) 'Rated Horsepower 160' and 7.5 'rated at 160 HP at 2700 RPM'.

maximum_rotation_speed.note: POH 2.7(d)(2) 'Maximum Rotation Speed (RPM) 2700'. One rating only; there is no separate lower maximum-continuous figure.

maximum_oil_temperature.note: POH 2.7(d)(3) 'Maximum Oil Temperature 245 deg F'. The OCR text layer renders this as '24SO F'; read directly off the rendered page as 245 deg F.

fuel_pressure_red_line_minimum.note: POH 2.7(f) 'Minimum (red line) .5 PSI'. Half a PSI, not 5.

fuel_pressure_red_line_maximum.note: POH 2.7(f) 'Maximum (red line) 8 PSI'. The OCR renders this as 'g PSI'; the rendered page reads 8.

fuel_grade.note: POH 2.7(g) 'Fuel (AVGAS ONLY) (minimum grade) 100 or 100LL Aviation Grade'. Section 8.21(b) is stricter in wording: 'The minimum aviation grade fuel for the PA-28-161 is 100.' TCDS 2A13 XVI-A says '100 octane minimum grade aviation gasoline'. Safe oral answer: minimum grade 100; 100LL is approved and is what is actually available.

fuel_colour.note: POH 1.7(c)(1) states it outright: 'Minimum Octane 100 Green or 100LL Blue Aviation Grade'. The Section 8 FUEL GRADE COMPARISON CHART, read off the rendered page, gives current commercial grades: 80 red, 100LL blue, 100 green, and previous grades 80/87 red, 91/96 blue, 100/130 green, 115/145 purple. Footnote: 'Grade 100LL fuel in some overseas countries is currently colored green and designated as 100L.'

type.note: POH 1.5(f) 'Propeller Type Fixed Pitch'. POH 7.5: 'The propeller is made of an aluminum alloy construction.' Fixed pitch is why RPM is the primary power indication and why the first sign of carb ice is an RPM drop.

diameter_maximum.note: POH 2.7(k) 'Maximum 74 IN.' and 1.5(e)(1). POH 7.5 adds 'The propeller has a 74-inch diameter with a 58 or 60-inch pitch. The pitch is determined at 75% of the diameter.'

static_rpm_74DM6_0_58.note: POH 2.7(m), same conditions and same NOTE.

tachometer_green_arc.note: POH 2.9(a) 'Green Arc (Normal Operating Range) 500 to 2700 RPM'.

oil_temperature_green_arc.note: POH 2.9(b) 'Green Arc (Normal Operating Range) 75 deg to 245 deg F'. THE OCR TEXT LAYER LEAVES THIS LINE BLANK; the numbers were read off the rendered page. This closes a gap the earlier research pass could not fill.

oil_temperature_red_line.note: POH 2.9(b) 'Red Line (Maximum) 245 deg F'. Agrees with the 2.7(d)(3) limit. Also blank in the OCR; read off the page.

oil_pressure_green_arc.note: POH 2.9(c) 'Green Arc (Normal Operating Range) 60 to 90 PSI'.

oil_pressure_yellow_arc_idle.note: POH 2.9(c) 'Yellow Arc (Caution Range) (Idle) 25 to 60 PSI'. There are TWO yellow arcs on this gauge - this one and the ground warm-up one. Favourite examiner question.

fuel_pressure_green_arc.note: POH 2.9(d) 'Green Arc (Normal Operating Range) .5 to 8 PSI'.

weight_limits_AS_PRINTED_IN_VB1180._WARNING: EVERY FIGURE IN THIS BLOCK IS A VB-1180 (serials 28-8316001 and up) FIGURE AND DOES NOT APPLY TO SERIAL 28-8116257. Recorded only so he can recognise it if he sees it in the wrong book. His figures are in weight_limits_FOR_HIS_SERIAL.

maximum_takeoff_weight_normal.note: POH 2.11(a) and 1.11(a), Normal column. NOT HIS AIRPLANE.

maximum_takeoff_weight_utility.note: POH 2.11(a) and 1.11(a), Utility column. This one happens to match the TCDS utility figure for his serial range, but confirm in VB-880.

maximum_ramp_weight_normal.note: POH 2.11(b) and 1.11(b). NOT HIS AIRPLANE. Note it is exactly gross + 7 lb, the start/taxi/run-up fuel allowance.

maximum_landing_weight_normal.note: POH 1.11(c), Normal column. Same as takeoff weight - there is no reduced landing weight on this airplane. NOT HIS NUMBER.

maximum_baggage_normal.note: POH 2.11(c) and 1.11(d), Normal column; the baggage door placard reads 'BAGGAGE MAXIMUM 200 LBS'; POH 7.1 and 7.27 both say 200 pounds. This is a structural/volume limit, not a gross-weight-derived one, so it carries across.

maximum_baggage_utility.note: POH 2.11(c), Utility column, and the baggage door placard: 'UTILITY CATEGORY OPERATION - NO BAGGAGE OR AFT PASSENGERS ALLOWED.'

note_printed.value: Refer to Section 5 (Performance) for maximum weight as limited by performance.

maximum_takeoff_weight_normal.note: FAA TCDS 2A13 item XVI-A, the item whose serial range (28-7716001 through 28-8216300) contains 28-8116257. THIS IS THE NUMBER HE USES. Do not quote 2440.

maximum_takeoff_weight_utility.note: FAA TCDS 2A13 item XVI-A. Same as the VB-1180 utility figure.

maximum_ramp_weight_normal.note: NOT PUBLISHED ANYWHERE AVAILABLE. The TCDS does not give a ramp weight and VB-1180's 2447 lb is the 2440 lb airframe's figure. High confidence that the value is UNKNOWN, not that any number is right. Piper's convention on this airframe is gross + 7 lb (the Section 6 start/taxi/run-up allowance), which would give 2332 lb, but that is arithmetic and must not be quoted as a limit. Get it from VB-880 Section 2.11.
maximum_ramp_weight_normal.src: Not published: absent from FAA TCDS 2A13 and from POH VB-1180 for his serial

maximum_baggage.note: The baggage limit is structural and is the same across the Warrior II serial range; VB-1180 2.11(c), the baggage door placard and TCDS all give 200 lb normal / 0 lb utility.

The 1950-and-less and 2020 rows describe weights his airplane can actually be at, and are very likely identical in VB-880 - but the forward limit at HIS 2325 lb maximum is not in this book and must come from VB-880 Figure 2.13 / the Section 6 envelope in his own handbook.

normal_category.note: POH 2.13(a), read off the rendered page (the OCR mangles 83.0/93.0 as '83n'/'93n'). Straight line variation between the points given. The 2440 lb row does not apply to him.

utility_category.note: POH 2.13(b). Both rows are at weights his airplane can legally be at and the utility gross is the same 2020 lb, so these very probably carry across - but confirm in VB-880.

moment_limits.note: VB-1180 DOES NOT PUBLISH A MOMENT-LIMIT TABLE. Section 2.13 gives CG limits in inches only; Section 6 works in weight-and-arm with a graphical C.G. ENVELOPE (Figure 6-15, captioned '2440 MAX. GROSS WT.') and a Loading Graph (Figure 6-13). No moment envelope with in-lb limits is printed. Anything he has seen in that form is from another source. The Figure 6-15 envelope is a 2440 lb envelope and is not his.

loading_arms.note: POH Figure 6-11 WEIGHT AND BALANCE LOADING FORM and Figure 6-9 sample problem. These are geometry (seat and tank positions), not weight limits, so they carry across. The -7 lb fuel allowance for engine start, taxi and run-up is what makes ramp weight exceed takeoff weight by 7 lb.

normal_category.value: All acrobatic maneuvers including spins prohibited.

utility_category_approved_maneuvers.note: POH 2.15(b) 'Utility Category - Approved Maneuvers for bank angles exceeding 60 deg'. THE THREE MANEUVERS CARRY ACROSS; THE 111 KIAS ENTRY SPEED DOES NOT - it is VA at 2440 lb, and at his 2325 lb gross it will be lower (about 108 KIAS by interpolation). Note the heading: these are the maneuvers approved for bank angles EXCEEDING 60 degrees, which is exactly the commercial steep turn / chandelle / lazy eight set.

spins.value: Prohibited in both normal and utility category
spins.note: POH 2.15(a) prohibits spins in normal category; the UTILITY CATEGORY OPERATION ONLY placard lists 'SPINS PROHIBITED' as the first line of the acrobatic maneuver list; the in-full-view-of-pilot category placard says 'SPINS ARE PROHIBITED FOR NORMAL AND UTILITY CATEGORY'; and POH 3.25 says 'Intentional spins are prohibited in this airplane.' Four places in the one book.

negative.note: POH 2.17(b) verbatim - the handbook does NOT publish a negative G number, it writes 'No inverted maneuvers approved' across both columns.

flaps_up_versus_flaps_down.note: VB-1180 DOES NOT PUBLISH SEPARATE FLAPS-UP AND FLAPS-DOWN LOAD FACTORS. Section 2.17 gives one pair of numbers (3.8 G normal, 4.4 G utility) with no flap qualifier. The commonly taught 2.0 G flaps-down figure comes from the certification rule (CAR 3 / FAR 23), not from this handbook. If the examiner asks, the correct answer is that the POH publishes 3.8 / 4.4 and does not break them out by flap position; do not quote 2.0 G as a POH figure.

approved.value: Day or night VFR, day or night IFR, when the appropriate equipment is installed and operable
approved.note: POH 2.19 verbatim: 'This airplane may be operated in day or night VFR, day or night IFR when the appropriate equipment is installed and operable.' No icing approval is stated anywhere in Section 2.

day_vfr_equipment.note: POH 2.19(a), all twelve items verbatim. Note items (7) fuel pressure indicator and (9) volt-ammeter - this list is a better answer to 'what instruments are required' for THIS airplane than reciting 91.205.

All equipment required for Day VFR
All equipment required for Day and Night VFR
All equipment required for Day IFR

note_printed.value: The above system and equipment list does not include specific flight instruments and communication/navigation equipment required by the FAR Part 91 and 135 operating requirements.
note_printed.note: POH 2.19 NOTE verbatim - i.e. the POH list is the type-certification basis, and 91.205 still applies on top of it.

mel_statement.value: Certain operations may be authorized with certain listed equipment and/or systems inoperative under certain conditions and under provisions defined by a current Minimum Equipment List (MEL) approved by the FAA which is dated concurrently with or after this Pilot's Operating Handbook and FAA Approved Airplane Flight Manual and authorized under an operating regulation which provides for use of an MEL.

unusable_fuel.note: POH 2.21(b) 'Unusable Fuel 2 U.S. GAL. The unusable fuel for this airplane has been determined as 1.0 gallon in each wing in critical flight attitude.' The qualifier matters - unusable is defined at the most critical flight attitude, not level flight.

usable_fuel.note: POH 2.21(c) 'Usable Fuel 48 U.S. GAL. The usable fuel in this airplane has been determined as 24.0 gallons in each wing.'

airspeeds._note: Section 2.3 prints only VNE, VNO, VFE and VA. VSO and VS1 are NOT printed as named speeds anywhere in Section 2; they are inferred from the airspeed indicator arcs and from the Section 4.37 text, and both are 2440 lb figures.

vne.note: POH 2.3 'Never Exceed Speed (VNE) - Do not exceed this speed in any operation.' A structural/flutter speed, independent of weight, so it carries across.

vno_maximum_structural_cruising.note: POH 2.3 'Maximum Structural Cruising Speed (VNO) - Do not exceed this speed except in smooth air and then only with caution.' VNO is defined at design gross weight; for a lighter maximum weight Piper normally publishes the same number, but confirm in VB-880.

vfe.note: POH 2.3 'Maximum Flaps Extended Speed (VFE) - Do not exceed this speed with the flaps extended.' Repeated in 4.5(d), in 7.9/10.3(c) and on the LANDING CHECKLIST placard ('Flaps - set (White Arc)').

va_at_2440.note: POH 2.3 'Design Maneuvering Speed (VA) - Do not make full or abrupt control movements above this speed. At 2440 LBS. G.W. 111 / 108.' DOES NOT APPLY TO HIS AIRPLANE - 2440 lb is not his gross weight.

va_at_1531.note: POH 2.3 'At 1531 LBS. G.W. 88 / 89'. Read directly off the rendered page; the KCAS figure really is printed higher than the KIAS figure at this end of the scale. 1531 lb is the low anchor of the VB-1180 interpolation line.

va_at_his_gross_2325_DERIVED.note: DERIVED, NOT A PUBLISHED FIGURE - do not quote it as a POH number. Linear interpolation on the VB-1180 line (88 KIAS at 1531 lb, 111 KIAS at 2440 lb, the handbook expressly permits 'Linear interpolation ... for intermediate gross weights') gives 108.1 KIAS at 2325 lb; the sqrt(W) rule gives 108.4. His own VB-880 will print its own VA at his gross weight and that is the number he must use.
va_at_his_gross_2325_DERIVED.src: Derived from POH VB-1180 2.3 p.2-2 and TCDS 2A13 XVI-A

va_caution_verbatim.value: Maneuvering speed decreases at lighter weight as the effects of aerodynamic forces become more pronounced. Linear interpolation may be used for intermediate gross weights. Maneuvering speed should not be exceeded while operating in rough air.
va_caution_verbatim.note: POH 2.3 CAUTION, transcribed verbatim from the rendered page.

turbulent_air_operating_speed.note: POH 4.5(c) 'Turbulent Air Operating Speed (See Subsection 2.3) 111 KIAS'. This is VA at 2440 lb under another name, so it inherits the same weight problem.

vso_stall_landing_config.note: NOT printed as 'VSO' anywhere. Two independent places in VB-1180 give 44 KIAS: the bottom of the white arc (2.5, 'White Arc (Flap Down) 44 to 103') and the Section 4.37 sentence 'The gross weight stalling speed with power off and full flaps is 44 KIAS.' Both are at 2440 lb gross.

vs1_stall_clean.note: NOT printed as 'VS1' anywhere. Inferred from the bottom of the green arc (2.5, 'Green Arc (Normal Operating Range) 50 to 126'), which by convention is VS1. At 2440 lb. Section 4.37 only says 'With the flaps up this speed is increased' without giving a number.

best_rate_of_climb_vy.note: POH 4.5(a) and 4.25 'The best rate of climb at gross weight will be obtained at 79 KIAS.' At gross weight - 2440 lb.

best_angle_of_climb_vx.note: POH 4.5(b) and 4.25 'The best angle of climb may be obtained at 63 KIAS.' At gross weight. 4.25 adds 'At lighter than gross weight these speeds are reduced somewhat.'

en_route_climb.note: POH Section 4 CLIMB checklist, 'En route 87 KIAS'.

final_approach_flaps_40.note: POH 4.5(e) 'Landing Final Approach Speed (Flaps 40 deg) 63 KIAS' and 4.31 'a final-approach speed of 63 KIAS with flaps extended to 40 deg'.

initial_approach.note: POH 4.31 'The airplane should be trimmed to an initial-approach speed of about 70 KIAS'.

best_glide.note: POH 3.13 'trim the aircraft for best gliding angle (73 KIAS)'; emergency checklist 'Trim for 73 KIAS'; 3.11 'An airspeed of at least 73 KIAS should be maintained'; Figure 5-33 associated conditions '73 KIAS'. Figure 5-33 states the chart weight as 2440 LBS, so 73 KIAS is a 2440 lb speed.

shortest_power_off_landing.note: POH 3.13 'When the field can easily be reached, slow to 63 KIAS for the shortest landing.'

open_door_speed.note: POH 3.27 'To close the door in flight, slow the airplane to 89 KIAS, close the cabin vents and open the storm window.'

normal_takeoff_rotation.note: POH 4.23 'Allow the airplane to accelerate to 45 to 55 KIAS depending on the weight of the aircraft and ease back on the control wheel to rotate to climb attitude.' Also 10.3(b): 'The best speed for takeoff is about 55 KIAS under normal conditions.'

max_demonstrated_crosswind.note: POH 4.5(f) 'Maximum Demonstrated Crosswind Velocity 17 KTS' and the cockpit placard 'DEMO. X-WIND 17 KTS.' A demonstrated value, not a limitation.

rated_rpm.note: POH 1.3(e) 'Rated Speed (rpm) 2700'; 2.7(d)(2); 7.5. Tachometer red line is also 2700 and is labelled 'Maximum Continuous Power', so there is no separate takeoff rating.

cylinders.note: POH 1.3(j) 'Four Cylinder, Direct Drive, Horizontally Opposed, Air Cooled'; 7.5 'a four cylinder, direct drive, horizontally opposed engine'.

configuration.value: Four cylinder, direct drive, horizontally opposed, air cooled
configuration.note: POH 1.3(j) verbatim. Direct drive means no reduction gearbox - propeller RPM equals crankshaft RPM.

bore.note: POH 1.3(f). Read off the rendered page - this is now a type-specific figure, not an inference from an O-320-H manual as in the earlier research pass.

compression_ratio.note: POH 1.3(i) 'Compression Ratio 8.5:1'. This is now confirmed from the handbook itself. It is the figure that distinguishes the 160 hp D-series from the 150 hp 7.00:1 E-series - the trap being that the 150 hp PA-28-151 Warrior and the 160 hp Warrior II look identical.

induction.value: Carbureted, updraft, through a chin scoop on the lower right cowling and a wetted polyurethane foam filter to the carburetor air box
induction.note: POH 7.5 verbatim: 'Carburetor induction air enters a chin scoop on the lower right cowling and is passed through a wetted polyurethane filter to the carburetor air box.' 7.5 also lists 'a wetted polyurethane foam induction air filter' in the engine equipment list. NOT fuel injected.

induction_air_filter.value: Wet-type polyurethane foam, located in the lower right front of the engine compartment, disposable, inspected at least once every 50 hours
induction_air_filter.note: POH 8.11 'The wet-type polyurethane foam air filter must be inspected at least once every 50 hours... The filter is disposable' and 'The filter is located in the lower right front of the engine compartment', secured by four quarter-turn fasteners. 8.11 also notes more frequent inspection may be necessary in dusty conditions.

carburetor.value: Float-type carburetor fed from a carburetor air box
carburetor.note: The POH names the carburetor throughout (7.5 'carburetor air box'; Figure 7-9 FUEL SYSTEM SCHEMATIC labels 'CARBURETOR' with THROTTLE and MIXTURE at it; 8.21(a) 'the fuel screens in the strainer, in the electric fuel pump, and at the carburetor inlet'). The POH does NOT state the carburetor make, model or float type; the TCDS gives the carburetor settings (10-5135 / 10-5009 / 10-5217). 'Float-type' is the standard Marvel-Schebler MA-4SPA on this engine but VB-1180 does not say so - do not assert the make in the oral.

carburetor_heat_source.value: A shroud around the muffler. Air for the muffler shroud is picked up from the nose cowling and carried through a duct to the shroud; heated air then enters the carburetor air box through a hose connected to the heater shroud.
carburetor_heat_source.note: POH 7.5 verbatim: 'The exhaust system is constructed of stainless steel and incorporates dual mufflers with heater shrouds to supply heated air for the cabin, the defroster system and the carburetor deicing system' and 'Air for the muffler shroud is also picked up from the nose cowling and carried through a duct to the shroud. Heated air enters the carburetor air box through a hose connected to the heater shroud.' THIS CLOSES THE GAP THE EARLIER PASS COULD NOT FILL. The same muffler shrouds feed cabin heat, defrost and carb heat.

carburetor_heat_air_is_unfiltered.note: POH 4.19 verbatim: 'Avoid prolonged ground operation with carburetor heat ON as the air is unfiltered.' CONFIRMED FROM THE HANDBOOK - the earlier pass could only offer this as a generic claim.

carburetor_heat_control.value: A lever to the right of the control quadrant on the instrument panel, placarded with two positions: ON (down), OFF (up)
carburetor_heat_control.note: POH 7.11 verbatim: 'The carburetor heat control lever is located to the right of the control quadrant on the instrument panel. The control is placarded with two positions: ON (down), OFF (up).' Two positions only - it is an on/off control, not a modulating one, which is why the POH insists on full heat.

carburetor_heat_use_full_not_partial.value: Always use full heat; partial heat may be worse than no heat at all
carburetor_heat_use_full_not_partial.note: POH 3.41 NOTE verbatim: 'Partial carburetor heat may be worse than no heat at all, since it may melt part of the ice which will refreeze in the intake system. Therefore when using carburetor heat always use full heat, and, when ice is removed, return the control to the full cold position.' Also 3.29: 'Carburetor heat should be full on when carburetor ice is encountered.'

magnetos.note: POH 7.5 lists the engine as 'equipped with a starter, a 60 amp 14 volt alternator, a shielded ignition, two magnetos, vacuum pump drive, a fuel pump, and a wetted polyurethane foam induction air filter.'

magneto_drive.note: VB-1180 DOES NOT STATE THE MAGNETO DRIVE ARRANGEMENT IN WORDS. 7.5 lists 'two magnetos' among the engine-driven accessories alongside the 'vacuum pump drive', which implies accessory-gear drive, but the handbook never says so. The safe oral answer is the principle: a magneto is engine driven and self-exciting, so it needs no electrical power and the engine will keep running with the master off. Do not claim a VB-1180 sentence for the drive detail.

impulse_coupling.value: Not described in VB-1180. Operating Tip 10.3(j) identifies the LEFT magneto as the one to use for starting, which is how an impulse-coupled magneto is used.
impulse_coupling.note: POH 10.3(j) verbatim: 'Hand starting of the engine is not recommended, however, should hand starting of the engine be required, only experienced personnel should attempt this procedure. The magneto selector should be placed to LEFT during the starting procedures to reduce the probability of "kick back." Place the ignition switch to BOTH position after the engine has started.' The words 'impulse coupling' appear NOWHERE in VB-1180 (searched the full text). The Lycoming O-320-D3G parts catalog lists one plain magneto (Slick 4370) and one impulse magneto (Slick 4371). Combining the two: one magneto is impulse coupled and the left-mag starting tip points to it being the left. He may say that; he may not claim the POH says 'impulse coupling', because it does not.

ignition_harness.note: POH 7.5 verbatim: 'It is equipped with a starter, a 60 amp 14 volt alternator, a shielded ignition, two magnetos...'. That is the only description of the harness in the handbook - the POH gives no plug count, no harness routing and no statement of which plugs each magneto fires. Shielding exists to keep ignition noise out of the radios.

spark_plugs_per_cylinder.note: NOT STATED IN VB-1180. The handbook never gives a plug count. Two per cylinder (eight total) is correct for the engine but it is not a POH fact, and the handbook does not say which plugs each magneto fires either. Say 'two per cylinder, one fired by each magneto, which I'd confirm from the engine manual' rather than inventing a top/bottom assignment.
spark_plugs_per_cylinder.src: POH VB-1180 (full text searched; no plug count appears)

magneto_vents.value: The magnetos have vents, which must be taped over before spraying solvent in the engine compartment
magneto_vents.note: POH 8.27(a) 'Before cleaning the engine compartment, place a strip of tape on the magneto vents to prevent any solvent from entering these units.' A small detail but it is a POH-sourced answer to 'do the magnetos breathe'.

exhaust.value: Stainless steel, incorporating dual mufflers with heater shrouds
exhaust.note: POH 7.5 verbatim: 'The exhaust system is constructed of stainless steel and incorporates dual mufflers with heater shrouds to supply heated air for the cabin, the defroster system and the carburetor deicing system.' Note the word Piper uses for carb heat: 'carburetor deicing system'.

cooling.value: Air cooled. Engine air enters on either side of the propeller through openings in a nose cowling and is carried through the engine baffling around the engine and oil cooler.
cooling.note: POH 1.3(j) 'Air Cooled' and 7.5 verbatim. There are NO COWL FLAPS on this airplane - cylinder cooling is managed with airspeed, mixture and climb angle. Note the baffling carries the cooling air both around the cylinders and to the oil cooler.

engine_mounts.value: Steel tubing, dynafocal mounts provided to reduce vibration
engine_mounts.note: POH 7.5 verbatim: 'The engine mounts are constructed of steel tubing, and dynafocal mounts are provided to reduce vibration.' POH 7.3 notes the steel tube engine mount is one of the few non-aluminium primary structures.

cowling.value: Cantilever structures attached at the fire wall, accessible for inspection through top-hinged side panels on either side

starter.value: Fitted; engaged by rotating the magneto/ignition switch clockwise
starter.note: POH 7.5 lists a starter among the engine equipment; POH 7.15 lists the starter first among the 'Standard electrical accessories'; POH 4.3/4.15 starting procedures say 'engage the starter by rotating the magneto switch clockwise. When the engine fires, release the magneto switch'. So the starter is spring-loaded off the ignition switch, not a separate button. Operating Tip 10.3(e): check radio, light and pitot heat switches off before starting 'so as not to create an overloaded condition when the starter is engaged.'

throttle_control.value: Lever on the control quadrant, lower centre of the instrument panel, accessible to both pilot and copilot; teflon-lined control cables; used to adjust engine RPM

mixture_control.value: Lever on the same control quadrant; adjusts the air to fuel ratio; the engine is shut down by placing the mixture lever in the full lean position
mixture_control.note: POH 7.11 verbatim: 'The mixture control lever is used to adjust the air to fuel ratio. The engine is shut down by the placing of the mixture lever in the full lean position.' 7.11 refers leaning technique to the Avco-Lycoming Operator's Manual.

friction_lock.value: A friction adjustment lever on the right side of the control quadrant, to increase or decrease friction holding the throttle and mixture or to lock them in a selected position

primer.value: An OPTIONAL engine priming system; the primer pump is immediately to the left of the throttle quadrant
primer.note: POH 7.13 verbatim: 'An optional engine priming system is available to facilitate starting. The primer pump is located to the immediate left of the throttle quadrant.' Note the word OPTIONAL - but the primer appears as item 30 on the typical instrument panel figure and 'Primer locked' is on the placarded TAKEOFF CHECKLIST and in the Before Takeoff and engine-failure checklists, so it is fitted in practice.

leaning_procedure.value: Reduce to the desired cruise power setting and lean the mixture to peak RPM; the POH refers detailed leaning to the Avco-Lycoming Operator's Manual
leaning_procedure.note: POH 4.27 CRUISING describes setting cruise power and leaning 'to peak RPM. Adjust the throttle, if necessary, for final RPM setting', and says leaning to peak engine RPM 'will provide best fuel economy'. POH 7.11 and 7.5 both refer the pilot to the Lycoming Operator's Manual. With no EGT fitted as standard, peak RPM is the POH's leaning reference on this airplane. POH 4.31 warns 'Full throttle operation with carburetor heat on can cause detonation.'

system_type.note: VB-1180 NEVER USES THE PHRASE 'WET SUMP'. The handbook describes an oil cooler, a dipstick and an 8-quart engine oil capacity, all of which are wet-sump features, and the Lycoming O-320 family is a wet-sump engine. Say 'wet sump - the sump is an integral part of the engine' and attribute it to the engine type, not to a POH sentence.
system_type.src: Inference from POH VB-1180 1.9, 7.5, 8.19; Lycoming O-320 series data (S7)

total_capacity.note: POH 1.9(a) 'Oil Capacity (U.S. quarts) 8' and 8.19 'The oil capacity of the engine is 8 quarts'. TCDS 2A13 independently: 'Oil capacity 8 quarts at (+27.5) (6 quarts usable)'.

minimum_for_flight.note: THE ANSWER TO THE QUESTION THREE SOURCES DISAGREED ON. POH 8.19, first sentence, verbatim: 'The oil capacity of the engine is 8 quarts, and the minimum safe quantity is 2 quarts.' Read off the rendered page (PDF 169). The POH calls it the MINIMUM SAFE QUANTITY. It is NOT the same thing as the TCDS's '6 quarts usable', which is a weight-and-balance figure, and it is NOT the 6-to-8-quart band some operators impose as local policy. He should give 2 quarts as the POH figure and add that his school's minimum is likely higher.

tcds_usable_oil.note: TCDS 2A13 item XVI-A: 'Oil capacity 8 quarts at (+27.5) (6 quarts usable)'. A WEIGHT AND BALANCE figure - it says how much of the 8 quarts is drainable/usable for loading purposes. Do not conflate it with the POH's 2-quart minimum safe quantity. Being able to separate these two numbers is exactly the kind of distinction that scores.

oil_arm.note: TCDS 2A13 'Oil capacity 8 quarts at (+27.5)'. Not printed in the POH Section 6 loading form, which treats oil as part of basic empty weight.

operator_preflight_band.note: NOT A POH FIGURE. One operator's (Lake Elmo Aero) PA28-161 checklist prints 'Oil Qty ... 6 to 8 Qts' as its preflight acceptance band. Offered only as a sanity check and clearly marked as school policy.

oil_cooler.value: Located on the left rear of the engine, mounted to the engine baffling. Engine cooling air, picked up in the nose section of the engine cowling and carried through the baffling, is utilized on the left side for the oil cooler.
oil_cooler.note: POH 7.5 verbatim. THIS CLOSES A GAP THE EARLIER PASS COULD NOT FILL. Note the cooler is cooled by the same baffled air that cools the cylinders - there is no separate scoop.

winterization_plate.value: A winterization plate is provided to restrict air during winter operation; the placard requires it to be removed when ambient temperature exceeds 50 deg F
winterization_plate.note: POH 7.5 'A winterization plate is provided to restrict air during winter operation (refer to Section 8)' plus the Section 2.25 placard 'OIL COOLER WINTERIZATION PLATE TO BE REMOVED WHEN AMBIENT TEMPERATURE EXCEEDS 50 deg F.' Relevant to a 24 November checkride - he should look for the plate on the preflight and know the rule.

thermostatic_bypass_vernatherm.note: NOT DESCRIBED IN VB-1180. The words 'vernatherm', 'thermostat' and 'bypass' do not appear in the handbook's oil discussion. Section 7.5 describes the cooler and the winterization plate and nothing else; Section 8.19 covers quantity, interval and grade only. A thermostatic bypass valve does exist on the Lycoming accessory housing, but that is an engine-manual fact, not a POH fact. CORRECT ORAL ANSWER: describe the cooler and the winterization plate from the POH, and say the thermostatic control of oil flow through the cooler is an engine-level detail he would confirm in the Lycoming manual. Do not guess at plumbing.

filter_or_screen.value: Full flow cartridge type oil filter, if fitted
filter_or_screen.note: POH 8.19 verbatim: 'It is recommended that the oil be drained and renewed every 50 hours and sooner under unfavorable operating conditions. Full flow cartridge type oil filters should be replaced each 50 hours of operation.' The handbook names a full-flow cartridge filter and does not describe a pressure-screen-only configuration, but it also does not state categorically that one is installed on every airframe. Which is actually on N84054 comes from the engine logbook and the accessory housing.

oil_change_interval.note: POH 8.19 'It is recommended that the oil be drained and renewed every 50 hours and sooner under unfavorable operating conditions. Full flow cartridge type oil filters should be replaced each 50 hours of operation.'

oil_and_filter_calendar_limit.note: POH 8.19 verbatim: 'The interval between oil and oil filter change is not to exceed four (4) months.' A full answer pairs the 50 hours with the four months.

lycoming_25_hour_screen_interval.note: NOT FROM THIS POH. Lycoming Service Bulletin 480 sets 25 hours with screen cleaning for engines with a pressure-screen system only, against 50 hours with a full-flow filter. VB-1180 8.19 publishes only the 50-hour/4-month figures. Offer the Lycoming qualifier as additional knowledge, attributed to Lycoming.

oil_specification.value: Refer to the latest issue of Lycoming Service Instruction 1014 (Lubricating Oil Recommendations)
oil_specification.note: POH 1.9(b) and the NOTE at the end of 8.19, both verbatim. The POH deliberately does not freeze a brand or specification - it points at the Lycoming SI, which is the right answer to 'what oil does it take'.

dipstick_and_filler.value: A dipstick, checked on the nose-section walk-around, which must be properly seated
dipstick_and_filler.note: POH 4.13 walk-around, nose section: 'Check the oil level, make sure that the dipstick has been properly seated.' The POH does NOT describe the filler neck, the dipstick markings or the access door beyond this. Do not describe a calibrated dipstick scale from memory.

breather.note: NOT DESCRIBED IN VB-1180. The handbook contains no description of a crankcase breather or its routing. An engine-manual item. Say so rather than guessing.

low_oil_pressure_warning.value: A low oil pressure indicator light on the annunciator panel
low_oil_pressure_warning.note: POH 7.15: 'The annunciator panel includes alternator and low oil pressure indicator lights.' POH 7.19: the annunciator panel 'is mounted in the upper instrument panel to warn the pilot of a possible malfunction in the alternator, oil pressure, or vacuum systems.' The light is a warning to go look at the gauge, not a diagnosis - see electrical.annunciator_panel.

oil_gauges_location.value: An engine cluster to the right of the pilot control wheel, including a fuel pressure gauge, a right and left main fuel quantity gauge, an oil temperature gauge and an oil pressure gauge
oil_gauges_location.note: POH 7.19 verbatim. Four of the gauges he will be asked about are in one cluster.

fuel._carries_note: VB-1180 7.13 is word-for-word the same text as the VB-880 Section 7.13 excerpt obtained in the earlier research pass (NTSB docket, revised 1981). The fuel system is identical. Highest confidence block in this file.

total_capacity.note: POH 7.13 'giving the airplane a total capacity of fifty U.S. gallons (48 gallons usable)'; 2.21(a); 1.7(a); TCDS 2A13 'Fuel capacity 50 gallons at (+95) (2 wing tanks)'.

unusable_capacity.note: POH 2.21(b): 'The unusable fuel for this airplane has been determined as 1.0 gallon in each wing in critical flight attitude.' One gallon a side, defined at the CRITICAL FLIGHT ATTITUDE, not in level flight. It is already excluded from the usable figure and included in empty weight, and must never be counted toward the 91.151 reserve.

number_of_tanks.note: POH 7.13 'two twenty-five gallon ... fuel tanks', one in each wing (7.3 'Each wing contains one fuel tank'). TCDS '(2 wing tanks)'.

capacity_per_tank.note: POH 7.13 verbatim: 'Fuel is stored in two twenty-five gallon (24 gallons usable) fuel tanks'. Also 8.21(c) 'Fuel is stored in two twenty-five gallon (24 usable) tanks.'

usable_per_tank.note: POH 7.13 '(24 gallons usable)'; 2.21(c) '24.0 gallons in each wing'. The fuel selector face itself is placarded 'L TANK 24 GAL' and 'R TANK 24 GAL' (Figure 7-7, read off the rendered page).

tab_capacity_per_tank.note: POH 7.13 verbatim: 'Each tank is equipped with a filler neck indicator tab to aid in determining fuel remaining when the tanks are not full. Usable capacity to the bottom of the indicator tab is 17 gallons.' VERY HIGH VALUE - 17 a side, 34 total, is how you fuel for a weight-limited flight, and it matters more on his 2325 lb airplane than on a 2440 lb one.

tank_arm.note: POH Figure 6-11 loading form 'Fuel (48 Gallon Maximum) ... 95.0'; TCDS 2A13 'Fuel capacity 50 gallons at (+95)'. Geometry, so it carries.

tank_construction.value: Secured to the leading edge of each wing with screws and nut plates, allowing removal for service or inspection
tank_construction.note: POH 7.13 verbatim. Note these are removable metal tanks, not bladders or wet wings.

positions.note: Three positions. Figure 7-7 FUEL SELECTOR, read off the rendered page (PDF 135), shows the face placarded 'L TANK 24 GAL' at the top left, 'R TANK 24 GAL' at the right, and 'FUEL OFF' at the lower left. POH 7.13 refers to moving the handle to the OFF position and back to the ON position.

has_both_position.note: THERE IS NO BOTH POSITION. Confirmed directly from the Figure 7-7 selector face. The single most reliable low-wing Piper question.

why_no_both.value: The POH does not state a design rationale.
why_no_both.note: EXPLANATION, NOT A POH QUOTE - and the handbook genuinely does not give one. The defensible, sourced half is the physical arrangement: the tanks are in the wings below the engine on a low-wing airplane, so fuel is drawn up by an engine-driven pump with an electric pump as backup (POH 7.13 and Figure 7-9), rather than gravity fed. Feeding both tanks through one suction line invites unporting and cross-feeding, so Piper requires one tank at a time and makes the pilot manage lateral balance. Present the mechanism as POH fact and the rationale as his own reasoning.

location.value: On the left side panel forward of the pilot's seat

off_detent.value: A button on the selector cover must be depressed and held while the handle is moved to the OFF position; the button releases automatically when the handle is moved back to the ON position
off_detent.note: POH 7.13 verbatim. A guard against inadvertently selecting OFF in flight. Worth knowing by feel.

switch_tanks_with_pump_on.value: ON for all takeoffs and landings and when switching tanks
switch_tanks_with_pump_on.note: POH 7.13. See electric_fuel_pump.when_on for the verbatim sentence.

purpose.value: Provided in case of the failure of the engine-driven pump
purpose.note: POH 7.13 verbatim: 'An auxiliary electric fuel pump is provided in case of the failure of the engine-driven pump.' Note what this does NOT say - it is a backup, not the normal supply and not a primer.

when_on_POH_SENTENCE_VERBATIM.value: The electric pump should be ON for all takeoffs and landings and when switching tanks.
when_on_POH_SENTENCE_VERBATIM.note: POH 7.13, third paragraph, transcribed verbatim from the rendered page (PDF 135). THIS IS THE SENTENCE THE EXAMINER WANTS. It is reinforced in three other places in the same handbook: the placarded TAKEOFF CHECKLIST ('Electric fuel pump on') and LANDING CHECKLIST ('Electric fuel pump on') in 2.25; the Before Takeoff checklist in 4.3; and 4.19, which adds the WHY - 'The electric fuel pump should be turned OFF after starting or during warm-up to make sure that the engine driven pump is operating. Prior to takeoff the electric pump should be turned ON again to prevent loss of power during takeoff should the engine driven pump fail.'

why_off_during_warmup.value: To make sure that the engine driven pump is operating
why_off_during_warmup.note: POH 4.19 verbatim: 'The electric fuel pump should be turned OFF after starting or during warm-up to make sure that the engine driven pump is operating.' This is the complete answer to 'why do you turn the boost pump off in the run-up' - it is a functional check of the engine-driven pump, and the Ground Check list has 'Electric fuel pump OFF' followed immediately by 'Fuel pressure check'.
why_off_during_warmup.src: POH VB-1180 4.19 p.4-19 (PDF 72); 4.3 GROUND CHECK p.4-8 (PDF 61)

switch_location.value: In the switch panel above the throttle quadrant

climb_off_point.note: POH Section 4 CLIMB checklist: 'Electric fuel pump ... OFF at desired altitude.'

emergency_use.note: From the Section 3 emergency checklists, read off the rendered pages. THE FIRE CASES ARE THE TRAP: both engine fire checklists turn the electric pump OFF and the fuel selector OFF, which is the opposite of every other fuel emergency.

engine_driven_pump.value: Fitted; the primary fuel pump in normal operation
engine_driven_pump.note: POH 7.5 lists 'a fuel pump' among the engine-driven equipment; Figure 7-9 FUEL SYSTEM SCHEMATIC labels 'ENGINE FUEL PUMP' in the line between the strainer and the carburetor (read off the rendered page, PDF 136); 7.13 refers to 'failure of the engine-driven pump'. The electric pump is in parallel, upstream of it on the schematic.

fuel_flow_path.value: Left or right main tank -> fuel tank selector valve -> fuel strainer -> electric fuel pump -> engine fuel pump -> carburetor, with a primer tap off the line between the strainer and the carburetor and a fuel pressure gauge at the carburetor
fuel_flow_path.note: Read off Figure 7-9 FUEL SYSTEM SCHEMATIC on the rendered page (PDF 136). The labelled items are: LEFT MAIN TANK, RIGHT MAIN TANK, FUEL TANK SELECTOR VALVE, FUEL STRAINER, ELECTRIC FUEL PUMP, ENGINE FUEL PUMP, PRIMER, CARBURETOR, FUEL PRESSURE GAUGE, FUEL QUANTITY GAUGES. A schematic reading, so the exact order of strainer vs electric pump is as drawn.

name.note: The POH's own word throughout - it does NOT use 'gascolator'. Use the POH's word.

location.value: On the lower left front of the fire wall, with a drain accessible from outside the nose section
location.note: POH 7.13 verbatim: 'A fuel strainer, located on the lower left front of the fire wall, has a drain which is accessible from outside the nose section.' POH 8.21(d) says the quick drain is 'located on the front lower corner of the fire wall'. POH 4.13 walk-around: 'Open the fuel strainer located on the left side of the fire wall'.

screens_cleaned.note: POH 8.21(a) verbatim: 'At every 50-hour inspection, the fuel screens in the strainer, in the electric fuel pump, and at the carburetor inlet must be cleaned.' THREE screens, not one - a strong answer.

count.note: Now definitively established from Section 8.21(d), read off the rendered page: 'Each fuel tank is equipped with an individual quick drain located at the lower inboard rear corner of the tank. The fuel strainer is equipped with a quick drain located on the front lower corner of the fire wall.' Two tank quick drains plus one strainer quick drain = THREE drain points. The earlier research pass could only record this at medium confidence because the walk-around prints 'Fuel tank sumps' in the plural; 8.21(d) settles it at one per tank. He should still count them on the airplane.

value: Left wing tank quick drain, lower inboard rear corner of the tank
Right wing tank quick drain, lower inboard rear corner of the tank
Fuel strainer quick drain, front lower corner of the fire wall
locations.note: POH 8.21(d) and 7.13, both verbatim as to location.

procedure_verbatim.value: The fuel system sumps and strainer should be drained daily prior to the first flight and after refueling to avoid the accumulation of contaminants such as water or sediment and for proper fuel. ... Each of the fuel tank sumps should be drained first. Then the fuel strainer should be drained twice, once with the fuel selector valve on each tank. Each time fuel is drained, sufficient fuel should be allowed to flow to ensure removal of contaminants. This fuel should be collected in a suitable container, examined for contaminants, proper fuel and then discarded.
procedure_verbatim.note: POH 8.21(d) verbatim. THE SEQUENCE IS THE SCORING DETAIL: tank sumps FIRST, then the strainer TWICE - once on each tank selection. Most candidates drain the strainer once. POH 7.13 adds: 'The fuel drains should be opened daily prior to first flight to check for water or sediment and proper fuel... The strainer should also be drained before the first flight of the day.'

value: When draining any amount of fuel, care should be taken to ensure that no fire hazard exists before starting the engine.
After draining, each quick drain should be checked to make sure it has closed completely and is not leaking.
Fuel additive cannot be used as a substitute for preflight draining of the fuel system drains.
cautions_verbatim.note: POH 8.21(d) CAUTIONS and the anti-icing additive CAUTION on p.8-12, all verbatim.

vents.value: One fuel tank vent per wing, checked clear of obstructions on the walk-around
vents.note: POH 4.13 walk-around, right wing and left wing: 'The fuel tank vent should be clear of obstructions.' VB-1180 Section 7 does NOT describe the vent type or location beyond this - there is no vent paragraph in 7.13. Purpose (maintain atmospheric pressure above the fuel as it is drawn off, so a vacuum cannot build and starve the engine) is standard reasoning, not a POH sentence.

location.value: Mounted in a gauge cluster on the left side of the instrument panel to the right of the control wheel, a right and a left main fuel quantity gauge
location.note: POH 7.13 'Fuel quantity and fuel pressure gauges are mounted in a gauge cluster located on the left side of the instrument panel to the right of the control wheel' and 7.19, which lists the engine cluster contents.

electrically_powered.note: POH 7.15 lists 'fuel gauge' among the STANDARD ELECTRICAL ACCESSORIES. So the gauges are lost with the electrical system - part of the alternator-failure answer. The POH does not describe the sender or gauge type.

cross_check_method.value: Open the fuel cap and visually check the fuel colour, and the quantity should match the indication that was on the fuel quantity gauge
cross_check_method.note: POH 4.13 walk-around, both wings, verbatim. THE POH ITSELF REQUIRES A VISUAL CROSS-CHECK OF THE GAUGE - that is a better answer than the folklore about gauges only being accurate at empty, which is a certification-rule claim and is NOT in this handbook.

known_inaccuracy_claim.note: THE 'ONLY ACCURATE AT EMPTY' CLAIM IS NOT IN THIS POH. Searched the full text; the handbook makes no statement about gauge accuracy. It comes from the certification rule, not from Piper. Safe answer: the POH requires a visual check against the gauge on every preflight (4.13), the tank has a 17-gallon indicator tab, and fuel is planned by known quantity on board plus time, with the gauge as a cross-check.

fuel_outlet_unporting_warning.value: Prolonged slips or skids which result in excess of 2000 ft. of altitude loss, or other radical or extreme maneuvers which could cause uncovering of the fuel outlet must be avoided as fuel flow interruption may occur when tank being used is not full.
fuel_outlet_unporting_warning.note: POH Operating Tip 10.3(i), verbatim. NOW SOURCED FROM THE WARRIOR II BOOK ITSELF rather than from the Warrior III handbook as in the earlier pass. Directly relevant to the commercial manoeuvres - steep spirals and prolonged slips - so it is a likely examiner bridge from the fuel system to the flight test.

fuel_caps.value: Optional locking fuel caps are available for all fillers; a single key will fit fuel caps, cabin door and baggage door compartments

anti_icing_additive.value: Approved. Must meet MIL-I-27686, uniformly blended with the fuel while refueling, not exceeding .15% by volume and not less than .10% by volume (about one and one half liquid ounces per ten gallons).
anti_icing_additive.note: POH 8.21 verbatim. CAUTION on the same page: 'Fuel additive cannot be used as a substitute for preflight draining of the fuel system drains.'

alternate_fuel.value: Whenever 100 or 100LL grade fuel is not available, commercial grade 100/130 should be used
alternate_fuel.note: POH 8.21(b) verbatim, which also refers to Lycoming Service Instruction No. 1070 and warns 'the use of lower grades can cause serious engine damage in a short period of time, the engine warranty is invalidated by the use of lower octanes.'

electrical._carries_note: The component list, ratings, switch and breaker locations and the ammeter description are the same system. ONE EXCEPTION, AND IT IS A REAL ONE: VB-1180 puts the battery on the forward right face of the fire wall, while the VB-880 Section 7.15 excerpt obtained in the earlier research pass puts it in a thermoplastic box immediately aft of the main spar. Piper moved the battery. See serial_caveats.

system_voltage.note: POH 7.15 verbatim: 'The electrical system includes a 14-volt, 60-amp alternator; a 12-volt battery; a voltage regulator; an overvoltage relay and a master switch relay.' Note the distinction an examiner may probe: a 14-volt CHARGING system supplying a 12-volt battery.

alternator_rating.note: POH 7.15 and 7.5 ('a 60 amp 14 volt alternator'). Two places in the handbook.

alternator_type_and_drive.note: VB-1180 DOES NOT STATE THE DRIVE in 7.5 or 7.15 - it gives the rating only. Belt drive is established indirectly from the POH's own walk-around: 4.13, nose section, 'check the alternator belt for proper tension'. That is a POH sentence and is enough to say belt-driven. The advantage over a generator worth stating: an alternator produces useful output at low engine RPM.

battery_voltage.note: POH 7.15 'a 12-volt battery' and 8.25 'Access to the 12-volt battery...'.

battery_capacity_amp_hours.note: NOT STATED ANYWHERE IN VB-1180. The handbook gives the voltage only; it never prints an amp-hour rating. Must be read off the battery label or the airplane's equipment list. Real Warriors fly with both 25 Ah and 35 Ah batteries.

battery_type.value: Lead-acid, flooded (serviceable with water, checked with a hydrometer)
battery_type.note: Inferred from POH 8.25, which is explicit about the servicing: 'The battery should be checked for proper fluid level. DO NOT fill the battery above the baffle plates. DO NOT fill the battery with acid - use only water. A hydrometer check will determine the percent of charge in the battery.' A battery you top up with water and check with a hydrometer is a flooded lead-acid cell. The POH never names the chemistry outright, and a sealed/RG battery may have been fitted since.

battery_location_VB1180.value: In a box, mounted on the forward right face of the fire wall; access by raising the upper right cowl and removing the cover of the battery box
battery_location_VB1180.note: POH 7.15 'The battery is in a box, mounted on the forward right face of the fire wall' and 8.25 'Access to the 12-volt battery is obtained by raising upper right cowl and removing the cover of the battery box, which is mounted on the forward right face of the fire wall.' TWO places in VB-1180 agree. BUT SEE THE NEXT ENTRY - this is NOT where his battery is.

battery_location_FOR_HIS_SERIAL.value: Aft of the main spar, under the rear seat area, per VB-880 - NOT on the firewall
battery_location_FOR_HIS_SERIAL.note: DIRECT CONFLICT AND A GENUINE AIRFRAME DIFFERENCE. The VB-880 Section 7.15 excerpt obtained in the earlier research pass (NTSB docket copy, revised 1981, the book that applies to 28-8116257) reads 'The battery is mounted in a thermoplastic box immediately aft of the main spar.' VB-1180 puts it on the forward right face of the firewall. Piper relocated the battery between the two serial blocks. HE MUST OPEN THE AIRPLANE AND LOOK, and he must not answer 'on the firewall' just because that is what the common online POH says. Consequences differ: an aft battery is a weight-and-balance item behind the CG and is not reachable in flight; a firewall battery is in the engine compartment.
battery_location_FOR_HIS_SERIAL.src: VB-880 Section 7.15 (NTSB docket, S3) vs POH VB-1180 7.15/8.25

battery_box_drain.value: The battery box has a drain tube which is normally closed off with a cap and which should be opened occasionally to drain off any accumulation of liquid
battery_box_drain.note: POH 8.25 verbatim. Applies to the VB-1180 firewall installation; whether his aft installation has the same arrangement is unverified.

battery_charging.value: If the battery is not up to charge, recharge starting at a 4 amp rate and finishing with a 2 amp rate. Quick charges are not recommended.

voltage_regulator.value: Fitted; located on the forward left side of the fuselage behind the instrument panel
voltage_regulator.note: POH 7.15 verbatim: 'The regulator and overvoltage relay are located on the forward left side of the fuselage behind the instrument panel.'

overvoltage_relay.value: Fitted; co-located with the regulator on the forward left side of the fuselage behind the instrument panel; resettable in flight by cycling the ALT switch
overvoltage_relay.note: POH 7.15 lists it among the system components and gives the location. POH 3.23 explains the reset: 'The next step is to attempt to reset the overvoltage relay. This is accomplished by... If the alternator failure was caused by a momentary overvoltage condition (16.5 volts and up) this procedure should return the system to normal.'

master_switch_relay.note: POH 7.15 lists 'a master switch relay' among the components. The POH gives no further description of it.

master_switch_is_split.note: Split into separate BAT and ALT halves. VB-1180 7.15 does not describe the switch itself, but the Section 3 procedures operate the halves independently and in opposition - ELECTRICAL FAILURES cycles 'ALT switch OFF ... ALT switch ON', and ELECTRICAL OVERLOAD commands 'ALT switch ON / BATT switch OFF'. You cannot write those checklists for a single-pole master. Figure 7-15 item 35 is the 'MASTER AND ACCESSORY SWITCH PANEL'. The VB-880 excerpt from the earlier pass adds that on some airframes the ALT half is mechanically interlocked with the BAT half; he should try moving ALT alone on the ground to see which his is.

why_split.value: So the alternator can be isolated without losing the battery
why_split.note: EXPLANATION, not a POH quote, but it is exactly what the Section 3 procedures do: ELECTRICAL FAILURES needs ALT off while BAT stays on to reset the overvoltage relay, and ELECTRICAL OVERLOAD needs BATT off while ALT stays on to shed a runaway regulator. He can justify the split purely from the two checklists in the book.

POH_SENTENCE_VERBATIM.value: Unlike previous generator systems, the ammeter as installed does not show battery discharge; rather, it indicates the electrical load on the alternator in amperes.
POH_SENTENCE_VERBATIM.note: POH 7.15, transcribed verbatim from the rendered page (PDF 138, printed 7-11, revised March 1, 2005). THIS IS THE SENTENCE. It is now quoted from a PA-28-161 Warrior II handbook, not inferred from a PA-28-140 or a PA-28R as in the earlier research pass. If he is asked 'does the ammeter show charge and discharge', the answer is no - it is a loadmeter.

what_it_reads.value: Load - the electrical load on the alternator, in amperes. It does NOT show battery discharge.
what_it_reads.note: See the verbatim sentence above. A candidate who answers 'it shows whether the battery is charging or discharging' has described a Cessna.

normal_indication_verbatim.value: With all the electrical equipment off and the master switch on, the ammeter will indicate the charging rate of the battery. As each electrical unit is switched on, the ammeter will indicate the total ampere draw of all the units including the battery. For example, the average continuous load for night flight with radios on is about 30 amperes. This 30 ampere value plus approximately 2 amperes for a fully charged battery will appear continuously under these flight conditions. The amount of current shown on the ammeter will tell immediately if the alternator system is operating normally, as the amount of current shown should equal the total amperage drawn by the electrical equipment which is operating.
normal_indication_verbatim.note: POH 7.15, continuing from the loadmeter sentence, verbatim from the rendered page. The 30 amp night-with-radios example and the 2 amp charged-battery figure are both POH numbers and are good detail to have ready.

typical_night_load.note: POH 7.15: 'the average continuous load for night flight with radios on is about 30 amperes.'

fully_charged_battery_draw.note: POH 7.15: 'This 30 ampere value plus approximately 2 amperes for a fully charged battery will appear continuously under these flight conditions.'

indication_on_alternator_failure.note: POH 3.23 verbatim: 'Loss of alternator output is detected through zero reading on the ammeter.' A centre-zero charge/discharge ammeter would swing to DISCHARGE, not to zero - so the zero-on-failure indication is itself proof the gauge is a loadmeter. Section 3 checklist: 'If ammeter shows zero: ALT switch OFF...'

required_equipment.value: A 'Volt-ammeter' is on the Day VFR required equipment list
required_equipment.note: POH 2.19(a)(9). Figure 7-15 item 36 calls it the 'ALTERNATOR GAUGE'. Note the handbook uses three names for the same area of panel - ammeter, volt-ammeter, alternator gauge.

value: Low vacuum (only when the optional gyro system is installed)
lights.note: POH 7.15 verbatim: 'The annunciator panel includes alternator and low oil pressure indicator lights. When the optional gyro system is installed, the annunciator panel also includes a low vacuum indicator light.' POH 7.19 confirms the panel warns 'of a possible malfunction in the alternator, oil pressure, or vacuum systems'. Identical to the VB-880 text.

what_the_lights_mean_verbatim.value: The annunciator panel lights are provided only as a warning to the pilot that a system may not be operating properly, and that he should check and monitor the applicable system gauge to determine when or if any necessary action is required.
what_the_lights_mean_verbatim.note: POH 7.15 verbatim. HIGH VALUE - the light tells you to look at the gauge; it is not itself the diagnosis.

false_alt_light_NOTE_verbatim.value: When operating with light electrical load and a fully charged battery, the Alternator Inop. light may illuminate due to minimal alternator output. If the alternator is functional a slight increase in electrical load should extinguish the Inop. indication.
false_alt_light_NOTE_verbatim.note: POH 7.15 NOTE, repeated word for word as the first NOTE in the Section 3 ELECTRICAL FAILURES checklist. A very strong answer: the first thing to do with an ALT light is add a little load and see if it goes out.

test.value: Press-to-test button; checked in the Ground Check
test.note: POH Section 4 GROUND CHECK 'Annunciator panel ... press-to-test'; 4.19 'Check the annunciator panel lights with the press-to-test button.' Also checked on the cockpit preflight with the master on. Figure 7-15 item 9 is the ANNUNCIATOR TEST SWITCH, item 10 the ANNUNCIATOR.

standard_electrical_accessories.note: POH 7.15 verbatim list. USE THIS FOR 'WHAT DO YOU LOSE IF THE ELECTRICS FAIL' - note the stall warning horn and the fuel gauges are on it, and the IGNITION IS NOT.

optional_electrical_accessories.note: POH 7.15 verbatim, plus 'Circuits will handle the addition of communications and navigational equipment.'

circuit_breakers_versus_fuses.value: Circuit breakers, located on the lower right instrument panel
circuit_breakers_versus_fuses.note: POH 7.15 'the circuit breakers are located on the lower right instrument panel (refer to Figure 7-13)'; 7.19 'The radios and the circuit breakers are located on the upper and lower right panel, respectively'. Figure 7-13 is the CIRCUIT BREAKER PANEL. NO FUSES are described anywhere in VB-1180. Airmanship from the handbook itself: Operating Tip 10.3(d), 'Before attempting to reset any circuit breaker, allow a two to five minute cooling off period.'

switch_locations.value: Electrical switches on the right centre instrument panel; circuit breakers on the lower right instrument panel; a rheostat switch on the left side of the switch panel controls the navigational lights and the radio lights, and a similar switch on the right side controls and dims the panel lights
switch_locations.note: POH 7.15 verbatim. Figure 7-15 item 35 is the MASTER AND ACCESSORY SWITCH PANEL.

bus_arrangement.value: A main bus plus an avionics bus fed through an optional radio master switch, with an emergency bus switch as a backup feed to the avionics bus
bus_arrangement.note: POH 7.19 verbatim: 'An optional radio master switch is located near the top of the instrument panel between the radio stacks. It controls the power to all radios through the aircraft master switch. An emergency bus switch is also provided to supply auxiliary power to the avionics bus in event of a radio master switch circuit failure. The emergency bus switch is located behind the lower right shin guard, left of the circuit breaker panel.' THIS CLOSES A GAP THE EARLIER PASS LEFT OPEN - the handbook does describe an avionics bus and an emergency bus switch. It still does not draw a formal bus diagram. He should find the emergency bus switch behind the lower right shin guard in N84054 and be able to point at it.

external_power.value: Piper External Power (PEP), optional, through a receptacle on the right side of the fuselage forward of the wing
external_power.note: POH 7.33 verbatim. 'An external battery can be connected to the socket, thus allowing the operator to crank the engine without having to gain access to the airplane's battery.' The Section 4 STARTING WITH EXTERNAL POWER SOURCE checklist runs master OFF, all electrical equipment OFF, terminals connect, plug insert, normal start, then plug disconnect and 'Master switch ON - check ammeter'.

indications.value: The ALT annunciator light illuminates and the ammeter reads zero
indications.note: POH 3.23: 'Loss of alternator output is detected through zero reading on the ammeter.' The checklist is headed 'ALT annunciator light illuminated:' and the first step is 'Ammeter ... Check to verify inop. alt.'

value: NOTE: When operating with light electrical load and a fully charged battery, the Alternator Inop. light may illuminate due to minimal alternator output. If the alternator is functional a slight increase in electrical load should extinguish the Inop. indication.
Ammeter .......... Check to verify inop. alt.
ALT circuit breaker .......... Check and reset as required
If alternator output cannot be restored, reduce electrical loads and land as soon as practical. The battery is the only remaining source of electrical power.
checklist_verbatim.note: POH Section 3.3 ELECTRICAL FAILURES, transcribed step by step from the rendered page (PDF 40, printed 3-5, revised March 1, 2005). The earlier research pass could only assemble this from fragments; this is the ordered checklist. Note the order: verify on the ammeter, ALT off, SHED LOAD FIRST, then check and reset the breaker, then ALT back on.

amplified_verbatim.value: Loss of alternator output is detected through zero reading on the ammeter. ... If no increase in the ammeter reading is noted, alternator failure can be confirmed. ... check the alternator circuit breakers for a popped circuit. The next step is to attempt to reset the overvoltage relay. ... If the alternator failure was caused by a momentary overvoltage condition (16.5 volts and up) this procedure should return the system to normal. If the ammeter continues to indicate ZERO output, or if the alternator will not remain reset, turn off the alternator switch, keep the electrical load to a minimum, and land as soon as practical.
amplified_verbatim.note: POH 3.23, assembled from the amplified paragraph on the rendered page. The 16.5 volts and up overvoltage threshold is a POH number.

kept: The engine - the magnetos are self-exciting and need no electrical power
The vacuum gyros - the vacuum pump is engine driven (7.17)
The flaps - they are manually controlled by a cable and handle (7.9)
Brakes - hydraulic, toe pedals and hand lever (7.7)
lost_as_the_battery_drains: Stall warning indicator (7.29 NOTE: 'The stall warning system is inoperative with the master switch OFF')
Radios, transponder and any electric turn indicator (7.19: the turn and slip indicator is electrically operated)

what_is_lost_and_kept.note: Assembled from the POH's own STANDARD ELECTRICAL ACCESSORIES list (7.15), the manual flap description (7.9), the engine-driven vacuum pump (7.17/7.19) and the 4.37 stall-warning NOTE. Structuring the answer as keep / lose / why is what distinguishes a commercial candidate. NO BATTERY ENDURANCE FIGURE IS PUBLISHED - do not quote a number of minutes.

trigger.value: Alternator output more than 20 amps above the known electrical load
trigger.note: POH 3.24, the heading itself: 'ELECTRICAL OVERLOAD (Alternator over 20 amps above known electrical load)'. The amplified text: 'If abnormally high alternator output is observed (more than 20 amps above known electrical load)...'

value: NOTE: Due to increased system voltage and radio frequency noise, operation with ALT switch ON and BATT switch OFF should be made only when required by an electrical system failure.
If alternator loads are not reduced:
Land as soon as possible. Anticipate complete electrical failure.
checklist_verbatim.note: POH Section 3.3 ELECTRICAL OVERLOAD, transcribed from the rendered pages (PDF 40-41, printed 3-5/3-6). THIS IS THE PROCEDURE WHERE THE SPLIT MASTER MATTERS MOST - ALT stays ON and BATT goes OFF, which is only possible with a split switch. 3.24 adds: 'continue to monitor the ammeter. If the alternator output... All electrical loads are being supplied by the alternator.' Note the two different urgencies: 'as soon as practical' if loads reduce, 'as soon as possible' if they do not.

construction.value: Primary structure is aluminum alloy except the steel tube engine mount, steel landing gear struts and isolated areas; lightweight plastics in the extremities (wing tips, engine cowling) and in nonstructural components

fuselage.value: Conventional semi-monocoque. A cabin door for entrance and exit on the RIGHT side; a baggage door aft of the rear seat
fuselage.note: POH 7.3 verbatim. ONE CABIN DOOR ONLY, on the right - a real consideration for emergency egress and for the open-door procedure.

wing_attachment.value: Cantilever wings attached to each side of the fuselage by insertion of the butt ends of the main spars into a spar box carry-through, located under the rear seat, which provides in effect a continuous main spar; also attached by an auxiliary front spar and a rear spar
wing_attachment.note: POH 7.3 verbatim. The rear spar 'in addition to taking torque and drag loads, provides a mount for flaps and ailerons.'

empennage.value: A vertical stabilizer, an all-movable horizontal stabilator, and a rudder

type.value: An all-movable horizontal stabilator of the flying tail design - one piece, no separate fixed stabilizer and elevator
type.note: POH 7.3 'an all-movable horizontal stabilator' and 7.9 'The horizontal surface (stabilator) is of the flying tail design with a trim tab mounted on the trailing edge.'

tab_POH_SENTENCE_VERBATIM.value: The stabilator incorporates an anti-servo tab which improves longitudinal stability and provides longitudinal trim. This tab moves in the same direction as the stabilator, but with increased travel.
tab_POH_SENTENCE_VERBATIM.note: POH 7.3, final paragraph, verbatim from the rendered page. PIPER'S OWN BOOK CALLS IT AN ANTI-SERVO TAB and states the same-direction movement explicitly - the earlier pass had to borrow this from the FAA handbook and a PA-28R manual. 'With increased travel' is the detail almost nobody has.

dual_function.value: Serves the dual function of providing trim control and pitch control forces
dual_function.note: POH 7.9 verbatim: 'This tab serves the dual function of providing trim control and pitch control forces.' Combined with 7.3: it increases the stick force the pilot feels (so an inherently over-sensitive all-moving tail gets its feel back), improves longitudinal stability, and doubles as the trim surface. KEY POINT: it moves the SAME way as the stabilator - a balance tab or servo tab moves opposite. He can prove he knows it on the walk-around by pushing the stabilator trailing edge down and showing the tab going down with it.

trim_control.value: A trim control wheel on the control console between the front seats. Forward rotation gives nose down trim and aft rotation gives nose up trim.
trim_control.note: POH 7.9 verbatim. Figure 7-3 is the FLIGHT CONTROL CONSOLE.

rudder_and_trim.value: The rudder is conventional in design and incorporates a rudder trim. The trim mechanism is a spring loaded recentering device, located on the right side of the pedestal below the throttle quadrant. Turning the trim control clockwise gives nose right trim and counterclockwise gives nose left trim.
rudder_and_trim.note: POH 7.9 verbatim, plus 7.7: 'A spring device is incorporated in the rudder pedal torque tube assembly to provide rudder trim.' So rudder trim is a spring bias on the pedals, not a trim tab on the rudder - a good distinction to be able to draw.

flight_controls_general.value: Dual flight controls as standard equipment; the flight controls actuate the control surfaces through a cable system

type.value: Manually controlled, mechanical; balanced and spring loaded to return to the retracted (up) position; extended by a control cable from a handle between the front seats
type.note: POH 7.9 verbatim: 'Manually controlled flaps are provided on the PA-28-161. The flaps are balanced and spring loaded to return to the retracted (up) position. A control handle, which is located between the two front seats on the control console (Figure 7-3), extends the flaps by the use of a control cable.' POH 7.3 calls them 'four-position wing flaps ... mechanically controlled by a handle located between the front seats.' NOT ELECTRIC - they survive an alternator failure.

positions_degrees.note: POH 7.9 verbatim: 'To extend the flaps, the handle is pulled up to the desired flap setting of 10, 25 or 40 degrees.' Three extended detents plus retracted; POH 7.3 calls them 'four-position wing flaps'. Section 4 refers to 25 degrees as 'the second notch'. NOW READ FROM THE WARRIOR II BOOK, not inferred from a PA-28R as in the earlier pass.

retraction.value: Depress the button on the end of the handle and lower the control

pitch_change.value: When extending or retracting flaps, there is a pitch change in the airplane. This pitch change can be corrected either by stabilator trim or increased control wheel force.

right_flap_as_step.value: When the flaps are in the retracted (up) position the right flap, provided with an over-center lock mechanism, acts as a step. NOTE: The right flap will support a load only in the fully retracted (up) position.
right_flap_as_step.note: POH 7.9 and its NOTE, verbatim. Repeated in 4.35 PARKING ('The flaps are locked when in the UP position and should be left retracted'), in the 4.33 STOPPING ENGINE NOTE, in the Section 4 preflight CAUTION, and in Operating Tip 10.3(c). FIVE places - Piper clearly had a problem with people standing on extended flaps.

vfe.note: POH 2.3, 4.5(d), 10.3(c) 'Flaps may be lowered at airspeeds up to 103 KIAS. To reduce flap operating loads, it is desirable to have the airplane at a slower speed before extending the flaps.'

takeoff_settings.note: From the POH's own TAKEOFF checklists and 4.23. 'Takeoffs are normally made with flaps up; however, for short field takeoffs and for takeoffs under difficult conditions, such as deep grass or a soft surface, total distances can be reduced appreciably by lowering the flaps to 25 degrees and rotating at lower airspeed.' NOTE THE TRAP: the POH's plain SHORT FIELD takeoff is accomplished WITHOUT flaps; it is the short field WITH OBSTACLE that uses 25 degrees. Most candidates say 25 for every short field.

landing_setting.value: Full flap (40 degrees) for short and slow landings; partial or no flaps may be desirable in strong crosswinds
landing_setting.note: POH 4.31: 'Normally, the best technique for short and slow landings is to use full flap and enough power to maintain the desired airspeed and approach flight path' and 'In high wind conditions, particularly in strong crosswinds, it may be desirable to approach the ground at higher than normal speeds with partial or no flaps.' Also 'Braking is most effective when flaps are raised and back pressure is applied to the control wheel.'

type.value: Fixed tricycle gear; three air-oil (oleo) struts
type.note: POH 7.7 'The fixed-gear PA-28-161...' and 'The three struts are of the air-oil type'.

value.main: Cleveland 6.00 x 6 on each main gear

tire_pressures.note: POH 7.7 'At gross weight, the main gear tires require a pressure of 24 psi, and the nose gear tire requires a pressure of 30 psi' and 8.23 'keep them inflated to the proper pressures - 30 psi for the nose gear and 24 psi for the main gear.' Note 7.7 qualifies it 'at gross weight' and 8.23 does not; 8.23 is the servicing instruction and gives flat figures.

strut_extension.unit: inches of strut exposure under normal static load
strut_extension.note: POH 7.7 'the normal static load extension being 3.25 inches for the nose gear and 4.50 inches for the main gear'. The Section 4 walk-around gives the tolerance: 'there should be 3.25 +/- .25 inches of strut exposure' for the nose and '4.50 +/- .25 inches' for each main.

nose_wheel_steering.value: Steerable through a 30 degree arc each side of center using the rudder pedals and brakes; a bungee in the steering mechanism reduces steering effort and dampens bumps and shocks during taxiing; later aircraft have the bungee removed and are steerable through a 20 degree arc each side of center. A shimmy dampener is also included in the nose gear.
nose_wheel_steering.note: POH 7.7 verbatim. WHICH ARC APPLIES TO N84054 IS UNVERIFIED - 'later aircraft' is undefined in the handbook. He should say 30 degrees with the bungee, 20 degrees without, and that he would confirm which his has.

type.value: Cleveland single disc hydraulic brake assemblies on the main gear
type.note: POH 7.7 verbatim. No brakes on the nose wheel.

actuation.value: Toe brake pedals attached to the rudder pedals, or a hand lever and master cylinder located below and behind the center of the instrument sub panel. Hydraulic cylinders are located above each pedal and adjacent to the hand brake lever.

fluid_reservoir.value: On the top left front face of the fire wall

parking_brake.value: Incorporated in the master cylinder; actuated by pulling back on the brake lever and depressing the knob attached to the left side of the handle. To release, pull back on the brake lever to disengage the catch mechanism and allow the handle to swing forward.

device_POH_SENTENCE_VERBATIM.value: An approaching stall is indicated by an audible alarm located behind the instrument panel. The indicator activates at between five and ten knots above stall speed.
device_POH_SENTENCE_VERBATIM.note: POH 7.29, the whole subsection, verbatim from the rendered page (PDF 149). THE 5-TO-10-KNOT MARGIN IS NOW A POH FIGURE - the earlier pass could only cite a simulator manual for it. POH 4.37 says the same: 'An approaching stall is indicated by a stall warning horn which is activated between five and ten KTS above stall speed.'

how_it_is_triggered.value: A detector (lift detector tab) that is lifted by the airflow; checked by turning the master switch ON and lifting the detector
how_it_is_triggered.note: POH 4.13/4.37 preflight: 'the stall warning system should be checked by turning the master switch ON, lifting the detector and checking to determine if the [horn sounds].' VB-1180 does NOT describe the mechanism or state which wing the detector is on. The Piper PA-28-family maintenance manual (Dakota) says the lift detector is on the leading edge of the LEFT wing with a tab extending beyond the leading edge. The stagnation-point explanation (as AoA rises the stagnation point moves down and aft, so the rising airflow lifts the tab and closes a switch) is standard reasoning, not a POH sentence.
how_it_is_triggered.src: POH VB-1180 4.37 p.4-25; Piper PA-28 family maintenance manual (S16)

electrical_dependency_verbatim.value: The stall warning system is inoperative with the master switch OFF.
electrical_dependency_verbatim.note: POH 4.37 NOTE, verbatim. Confirmed by 7.15, which lists the 'stall warning indicator' among the STANDARD ELECTRICAL accessories. Consequence: lose all electrical power and you lose the stall warning.

stall_characteristics.value: Conventional. Mild airframe buffeting and gentle pitching may also precede the stall. The gross weight stalling speed with power off and full flaps is 44 KIAS. With the flaps up this speed is increased. Loss of altitude during stalls varies from 100 to 275 feet, depending on configuration and power.
stall_characteristics.note: POH 4.37 verbatim. The 44 KIAS and the 100-275 ft altitude loss are 2440 lb figures.

arrangement.value: A single pitot head on the bottom of the left wing supplies BOTH pitot and static pressure, carried through pitot and static lines within the wing and fuselage to the gauges
arrangement.note: POH 7.21 verbatim: 'Pitot and static pressure are picked up by a pitot head installed on the bottom of the left wing and carried through pitot and static lines within the wing and fuselage to the gauges on the instrument panel.' IMPORTANT AND OFTEN MISSED: THERE ARE NO FUSELAGE STATIC PORTS on this airplane - the static source is part of the wing-mounted head. The walk-around confirms it: 'Remove the cover from the pitot/static head on the underside of the wing.'

instruments_served.note: POH 7.21 'The system supplies both pitot and static pressure for the airspeed indicator, altimeter, and the optional vertical speed indicator (Figure 7-17).'

alternate_static_source.value: Available as OPTIONAL equipment. The control valve is located below the left side of the instrument panel.
alternate_static_source.note: POH 7.21 verbatim: 'An alternate static source is available as optional equipment. The control valve is located below the left side of the instrument panel. When the valve is set in the alternate position, the altimeter, vertical speed indicator and airspeed indicator will be using cabin air for static pressure. The storm window and cabin vents must be closed and the cabin heater and defroster must be on during alternate static source operation. The altimeter error is less than 50 feet unless otherwise placarded.' Figure 7-17 labels item 7 as ALTERNATE STATIC SOURCE. THE OPERATING CONDITIONS ARE THE SCORING DETAIL: storm window and cabin vents CLOSED, heater and defroster ON, altimeter error under 50 ft. IT IS OPTIONAL - he must look below the left side of the panel in N84054 and confirm whether one is fitted. If there is none, the answer to a blocked static source is to break the VSI glass.

drains.value: Both the pitot and static lines can be drained through separate drain valves located on the left lower side of the fuselage interior
drains.note: POH 7.21 verbatim. The cockpit preflight says 'Open the pitot and static drains to remove any moisture that has accumulated in the lines.' Figure 7-17 item 6 is DRAIN VALVES.

pitot_heat.value: A heated pitot head, which alleviates problems with icing and heavy rain, is available as OPTIONAL equipment. The switch is on the electrical switch panel to the left of the right control wheel.
