pitot_heat.note: POH 7.21 verbatim. Figure 7-17 item 3 is PITOT HEAT SWITCH. It is an electrical load - one of the first things to shed after an alternator failure, and Operating Tip 10.3(e) says to have it off before engaging the starter.

blockage.value: A partially or completely blocked pitot head will give erratic or zero readings on the instruments. To prevent bugs and water from entering the pitot and static pressure holes, a cover should be placed over the pitot head. NOTE: During the preflight, check to make sure the pitot cover is removed.

static_wicks.value: Static wicks on both wings, checked on the walk-around for firm attachment and good condition
static_wicks.note: POH 4.13 walk-around, right and left wing. THESE ARE NOT PART OF THE STATIC SYSTEM - they are precipitation-static dischargers for radio noise. Confusing them with static ports is an easy trap, made easier here by the fact that this airplane has no fuselage static ports at all.

status.note: POH 7.17 carries an asterisk and the footnote '*Optional equipment' at the bottom of printed page 7-13. Consistent with 7.19, which lists the attitude gyro, directional gyro and suction gauge as 'Instrument options available for the panel'. For IFR it is required - POH 2.19(c) lists a vacuum pump and gyro suction indicator as Day IFR equipment.

purpose_and_components.value: Designed to operate the air-driven gyro instruments, including the directional and attitude gyros when installed. The system consists of an engine driven vacuum pump, a vacuum regulator, a filter and the necessary plumbing.

what_it_drives.note: POH 7.17 and 7.19: 'The attitude gyro and directional gyro are vacuum operated through the use of a vacuum pump installed on the engine, while the turn and slip indicator is electrically operated.' THE SPLIT IS DELIBERATE - vacuum drives two gyros, electricity drives the third, so a single system failure leaves one gyro source. NOW CONFIRMED FROM THE WARRIOR II BOOK rather than a PA-28R handbook.

pump_type.value: A dry-type pump, engine driven, with a shear drive. If the drive shears, the gyros will become inoperative.
pump_type.note: POH 7.17 verbatim: 'The vacuum pump is a dry-type pump. A shear drive protects the pump from damage. If the drive shears, the gyros will become inoperative.' ENGINE DRIVEN is the point for the oral - the gyros survive an alternator failure.

normal_indication.note: POH 7.17 verbatim: 'The valve is set so the normal vacuum reads 4.8 to 5.1 inches of mercury, a setting which provides sufficient vacuum to operate all the gyros at their rated RPM.' The Section 4 GROUND CHECK agrees exactly: 'Vacuum ... 4.8" - 5.1" HG', and 4.19 adds 'the indicator should read 4.8" - 5.1" Hg at 2000 RPM'. NOTE IT IS 5.1, NOT 5.2 - the earlier pass had 4.8-5.2 from an operator checklist. Three places in the POH give 5.1.

regulator.value: A vacuum regulator is provided in the system to protect the gyros, located behind the instrument panel. Higher settings will damage the gyros and with a low setting the gyros will be unreliable.

failure_indications_verbatim.value: A decrease in pressure in a system that remained constant over an extended period may indicate a dirty filter, dirty screens, possibly a sticky vacuum regulator or leak in the system (a low vacuum indicator light is provided in the annunciator panel). Zero pressure would indicate a sheared pump drive, defective pump, possibly a defective gauge or collapsed line. In the event of any gauge variation from the norm, the pilot should have a mechanic check the system to prevent possible damage to the system components or eventual failure of the system.
failure_indications_verbatim.note: POH 7.17, verbatim across printed pages 7-13 and 7-14. A COMPLETE DIAGNOSTIC ANSWER FROM THE HANDBOOK ITSELF - gradual decrease means filter/screens/regulator/leak, zero means sheared drive/dead pump/bad gauge/collapsed line. The earlier pass recorded this as unverified.

normal_low_readings.value: Vacuum pressure, even though set correctly, can read lower at very high altitude (above 12,000 ft), and at low engine RPM (usually on approach or during training maneuvers). This is normal and should not be considered a malfunction.
normal_low_readings.note: POH 7.17 verbatim. Worth knowing for the checkride itself - low suction during slow flight is expected, not a failure.

low_vacuum_light.value: A low vacuum indicator light is provided in the annunciator panel when the optional gyro system is installed

heat_source_POH_SENTENCE.value: Heat for the cabin interior and the defroster system is provided by a shroud attached to the muffler.
heat_source_POH_SENTENCE.note: POH 7.23 verbatim. Combined with 7.5 ('dual mufflers with heater shrouds to supply heated air for the cabin, the defroster system and the carburetor deicing system'), the exhaust shrouds feed all three. THE SAFETY POINT HE SHOULD MAKE: heat comes from air passed over the exhaust, so a cracked muffler or exhaust can put carbon monoxide into the cabin, and the Section 3 answer to smoke or fumes includes cabin heat OFF and vents open.

controls.value: Heat controls on the far right side of the instrument panel; heat diversion controls on either side of the console atop the heat ducts regulate airflow between front and rear seats
controls.note: POH 7.23 verbatim. Figure 7-19 labels HEATER CONTROL, DEFROSTER CONTROL and CABIN HEAT DIVERSION CONTROL.

caution_verbatim.value: When cabin heat is operated, heat duct surface becomes hot. This could result in burns if arms or legs are placed too close to heat duct outlets or surface.

fresh_air.value: Fresh air inlets in the leading edges of the wings near the fuselage; an adjustable fresh air outlet at each front seat location on the side of the cabin near the floor; rear seat vents optional; cabin air is exhausted through an outlet located below the rear seat
fresh_air.note: POH 7.23 verbatim. The walk-around checks 'that the fresh air inlet is clear of foreign matter' on both wings.

overhead_vent_and_blower.value: An optional overhead ventilating system with outlets over each seat; on models without air conditioning an optional cabin air blower operated by a four-position fan switch - OFF, LOW, MED, HIGH

seats.value: Front seats adjustable fore and aft; the right front seat tilts forward to allow easy entry to the rear seats; optional headrests and optional vertical adjustment

shoulder_harnesses_verbatim.value: Shoulder harnesses with inertia reels are provided for each front seat occupant and, depending on the model year, are provided as standard or optional equipment for the occupants of the rear seats. A check of the inertia reel mechanism can be made by pulling sharply on the strap and checking that the reel will lock in place under sudden stress. This locking feature prevents the strap from extending and holds the occupant in place. Under normal movement the strap will extend and retract as required. Shoulder harnesses should be routinely worn during takeoff, landing and whenever an inflight emergency situation occurs.
shoulder_harnesses_verbatim.note: POH 7.25/7.26, verbatim. 'Depending on the model year' is a live caveat for a 1981 airframe - rear shoulder harnesses may or may not be fitted. The Before Takeoff procedure requires 'Pull test the locking restraint feature of the shoulder harness inertia reel' and 'Fasten the seat belts snugly around the empty seats.'

required_equipment.value: Safety restraint - each occupant, on the Day VFR required equipment list

cabin_door.value: One cabin door, on the RIGHT side of the airplane, double latched (an upper latch and a side latch)
cabin_door.note: POH 7.3 'On the right side of the airplane is a cabin door for entrance and exit.' POH 3.27 'The cabin door on the Cherokee is double latched, so the chance of it springing open in flight at both the top and side are remote.' Placard adjacent to the upper door latch: 'ENGAGE LATCH BEFORE FLIGHT'.

open_door_in_flight.value: A partially open door will not affect normal flight characteristics, and a normal landing can be made with the door open. If both upper and side latches are open, the door will trail slightly open and airspeed will be reduced slightly. To close in flight: slow to 89 KIAS, close the cabin vents, open the storm window; if the top latch is open, latch it; if the side latch is open, pull on the arm rest while moving the latch handle to the latched position; if both are open, close the side latch then the top latch.
open_door_in_flight.note: POH 3.27 verbatim. THE ORDER MATTERS - side latch first, then top. And the headline answer is that it is a nuisance, not an emergency: fly the airplane and land normally.

baggage_door.value: A large 20 x 22 inch outside baggage door on the right side of the fuselage, aft of the rear seat; a single key fits the fuel caps, cabin door and baggage door

storm_window.value: A pilot storm window is included in the cabin interior
storm_window.note: POH 7.25. Used in the open-door procedure and must be CLOSED for alternate static source operation (7.21).

volume.note: POH 7.27 'A 24 cubic foot baggage area, located behind the rear seat' and 1.15(a) 'Compartment Volume (cubic feet) 24'.

maximum_capacity.note: POH 7.27 'Maximum capacity is 200 pounds', 7.1, 2.11(c), 1.11(d) and the baggage door placard. Structural, so it carries across - but on a 2325 lb airplane he will run out of gross weight long before he runs out of baggage allowance.

utility_category.note: POH 2.11(c) Utility column and the baggage door placard: 'UTILITY CATEGORY OPERATION - NO BAGGAGE OR AFT PASSENGERS ALLOWED.'

access_and_restraint.value: Accessible from the cabin or loaded through the outside baggage door. Tie-down straps are available and they should be used at all times. NOTE: It is the pilot's responsibility to be sure when the baggage is loaded that the aircraft C.G. falls within the allowable C.G. range.

printed_error_in_1_15.value: POH 1.15 BAGGAGE SPACE prints '(b) Maximum Ramp Weight (lbs) 22' and '(c) Maximum Landing Weight (lbs) 20'
printed_error_in_1_15.note: A TYPESETTING ERROR IN THE HANDBOOK ITSELF, confirmed on the rendered page (PDF 15). Those two labels are copied from 1.11 by mistake; 22 and 20 are plainly the baggage door dimensions (7.27 gives 'a large 20 x 22 inch outside baggage door'). Recorded so he is not caught out by it, and because spotting it is a nice piece of evidence that he actually read the book.

engine_cluster.value: To the right of the pilot control wheel; includes a fuel pressure gauge, a right and left main fuel quantity gauge, an oil temperature gauge and an oil pressure gauge

value: Turn and slip indicator or turn coordinator
optional_instruments.note: POH 7.19 verbatim: 'Instrument options available for the panel includes a suction gauge, vertical speed indicator, attitude gyro, directional gyro, clock, tru-speed indicator and a turn and slip indicator or turn coordinator.' The vacuum suction gauge is on the far right of the instrument panel.

emergency_locator_transmitter.value: Optional. Located in the aft portion of the fuselage just below the stabilator leading edge, accessible through a plate on the right side of the fuselage attached with slotted-head nylon screws. Three position switch ON / OFF / ARM on the unit, normally ARM. A pilot's remote switch on the left side panel, placarded ON and ARM(ED), normally in the ARM position. The POH says the ELT meets the requirements of FAR 91.52.
emergency_locator_transmitter.note: POH 7.35 verbatim. Two ELT variants are documented, NARCO ELT 10 (p.7-24) and NARCO ELT 910 (p.7-24a) - which is fitted to N84054 is unverified. Battery replacement rules: replaced on or before the marked date, after any emergency use, if accumulated test time exceeds one hour, or after inadvertent activation for an undetermined period. Test transmissions only in the first five minutes of any hour, limited to three audio sweeps. NOTE: 'FAR 91.52' is the pre-1989 numbering; the current rule is 91.207.

carburetor_ice_detection_system.value: Optional. A control box on the instrument panel, a probe sensor mounted in the carburetor and a red warning light to indicate the presence of ice in the carburetor. WARNING: This instrument is approved as optional equipment only and Flight Operations should not be predicated on its use.
carburetor_ice_detection_system.note: POH 7.39 verbatim including the WARNING. Adjustment: master switch on, ice detection unit on, sensitivity knob fully counterclockwise until the carb ice light comes on, then back clockwise until it just goes out - that is the critical setting. 'If ice is present apply full carburetor heat.'

air_conditioning.value: Optional, a recirculating air system; evaporator behind the left rear side of the baggage compartment, condenser on a retractable scoop on the bottom of the fuselage aft of the baggage area, compressor on the forward right underside of the engine with an electric clutch. A DOOR OPEN indicator light to the left of the radio stack illuminates whenever the condenser door is open. At full throttle a micro switch disengages the compressor and retracts the scoop to obtain maximum power and rate of climb.
air_conditioning.note: POH 7.37 verbatim in substance. Relevant only if fitted; if it is, the AIR COND OFF items on the placarded takeoff and landing checklists become mandatory and the 'AIR CONDITIONER MUST BE OFF TO INSURE NORMAL TAKEOFF CLIMB PERFORMANCE' placard applies.

finish.value: All exterior surfaces primed with etching primer and finished with acrylic lacquer; an optional polyurethane finish is available

emergency._carries_note: Procedures (the ordered steps) carry across; the SPEEDS in them (73 KIAS glide, 63 KIAS shortest landing, 89 KIAS door) are 2440 lb figures and are marked individually.

general_statement.value: These procedures are suggested as a course of action for coping with the particular condition described, but are not a substitute for sound judgment and common sense. The first portion of this section consists of an abbreviated emergency check list which supplies an action sequence for critical situations with little emphasis on the operation of systems. The remainder of the section is devoted to amplified emergency procedures.
general_statement.note: POH 3.1, condensed from the verbatim text.

engine_fire_during_start.note: POH 3.3 verbatim. THE LOGIC IS WORTH SAYING OUT LOUD: keep cranking so the engine draws the fire into the cylinders and burns it; mixture to idle cut-off and fuel selector off to cut the supply; throttle open to maximise airflow.

value: If sufficient runway remains for a normal landing, land straight ahead.
If insufficient runway remains: maintain safe airspeed; make only shallow turn to avoid obstructions; flaps as situation requires.

If sufficient altitude has been gained to attempt a restart: maintain safe airspeed; Fuel selector .......... switch to tank containing fuel; Electric fuel pump .......... check ON; Mixture .......... check RICH; Carburetor heat .......... ON; Primer .......... locked
If power is not regained, proceed with power off landing.
engine_power_loss_during_takeoff.note: POH 3.3 verbatim. NOTE WHAT IT DOES NOT SAY: there is no 'turn back' option and no specified altitude for one - the POH says land straight ahead or make only a SHALLOW turn to avoid obstructions. 3.9 adds that if fuel exhaustion caused it, power will not be regained after switching tanks until the empty fuel lines fill, 'This may require up to ten seconds.'

value: Fuel selector .......... switch to tank containing fuel
Engine gauges .......... check for indication of cause of power loss
If no fuel pressure is indicated, check tank selector position to be sure it is on a tank containing fuel.
When power is restored: Carburetor heater .......... OFF; Electric fuel pump .......... OFF
If power is not restored, prepare for power off landing. Trim for 73 KIAS
engine_power_loss_in_flight.note: POH 3.3 verbatim. 3.11 amplifies: 'Complete engine power loss is usually caused by fuel flow interruption, and power will be restored shortly after fuel flow is restored... An airspeed of at least 73 KIAS should be maintained.' If time permits: ignition L then R then BOTH; move throttle and mixture to different settings, which 'may restore power if the problem is too rich or too lean a mixture or if there is a partial fuel system restriction'; try other fuel tanks; allow the engine to windmill if water is suspected - 'If power loss is due to water, fuel pressure indications will be normal.'

value: 1000 ft. above field at downwind position for normal landing approach.
When field can easily be reached slow to 63 KIAS for shortest landing.
Touchdowns should normally be made at lowest possible airspeed with full flaps.
When committed to landing: Ignition .......... OFF; Master switch .......... OFF; Fuel selector .......... OFF; Mixture .......... idle cut-off; Seat belts and harnesses .......... tight
power_off_landing.note: POH 3.3 verbatim. 3.13 amplifies: 'trim the aircraft for best gliding angle (73 KIAS)'; 'Excess altitude may be lost by widening your pattern, using flaps or slipping, or a combination of these.' THE 1000 FT AT THE DOWNWIND POSITION IS A SPECIFIC POH NUMBER worth quoting.

glide_speed.note: POH 3.13 'best gliding angle (73 KIAS)'. AT 2440 LB - the Figure 5-33 glide chart states 'WEIGHT 2440 LBS'. At his lighter maximum weight the best glide speed is lower; VB-880 will print its own.

glide_ratio.note: VB-1180 DOES NOT PUBLISH A GLIDE RATIO. Figure 5-33 GLIDE PERFORMANCE is a graph, with associated conditions 'WEIGHT 2440 LBS. PROP WINDMILLING / FLAPS 0 deg NO WIND / 73 KIAS' and a worked example: 'Cruise pressure altitude: 5000 ft. Terrain pressure altitude: 2000 ft. Glide distance (9.5 miles minus 3.9 miles): 5.6 nautical miles.' That example implies about 11.3:1 (3000 ft lost for 5.6 nm), but THAT IS ARITHMETIC OFF A CHART EXAMPLE, not a published ratio. If asked, he should say the POH gives a glide chart at 73 KIAS, prop windmilling, flaps up, and quote the chart example rather than a ratio - or give a rule of thumb clearly labelled as such (roughly 1.5 nm per 1000 ft).

first_step.note: POH 3.3. 3.15: 'The presence of fire is noted through smoke, smell and heat in the cabin. It is essential that the source of the fire be promptly identified through instrument readings, characteristics of the smoke, or other indications since the action to be taken differs somewhat in each case.'

electrical_fire.note: POH 3.3 verbatim, headed 'Electrical fire (smoke in cabin):'. NOTE THE CONSEQUENCE OF MASTER OFF on this airplane: he loses the electric fuel pump, the stall warning horn, the fuel gauges and the radios, but the engine keeps running on the magnetos and the vacuum gyros keep running on the engine-driven pump.

value: Proceed with POWER OFF LANDING procedure.
engine_fire.note: POH 3.3 verbatim. 3.15 adds 'If radio communication is not required, select master switch OFF.' THE ELECTRIC FUEL PUMP GOES OFF HERE - the opposite of every other fuel emergency, and where candidates get caught. The heater and defroster go off because their air comes from a shroud on the muffler, right next to the fire. NOTE (3.15): 'The possibility of an engine fire in flight is extremely remote. The procedure given is general and pilot judgement should be the determining factor for action in such an emergency.'

value: Land as soon as possible and investigate cause.
loss_of_oil_pressure.note: POH 3.3 verbatim - only two lines. 3.17 amplifies and is worth knowing in full: 'A partial loss of oil pressure usually indicates a malfunction in the oil pressure regulating system, and a landing should be made as soon as possible to investigate the cause and prevent engine damage. A complete loss of oil pressure indication may signify oil exhaustion or may be the result of a faulty gauge... the engine may stop suddenly. Maintain altitude until such time as a dead stick landing can be accomplished. Don't change power settings unnecessarily, as this may hasten complete power loss.' And: it may be advisable to make an off-airport landing while power is still available, 'particularly if other indications of actual oil pressure loss, such as sudden increases in temperatures, or oil smoke, are apparent, and an airport is not close.'

value: Fuel selector .......... check on full tank
Land at nearest airport and investigate the problem.

electrical_failures.note: The full ordered checklist is recorded under electrical.alternator_failure.

electrical_overload.note: The full ordered checklist is recorded under electrical.electrical_overload.

prohibition.value: Intentional spins are prohibited in this airplane.
prohibition.note: POH 3.25, first sentence, verbatim. Also 2.15(a), the category placard and the utility placard.

value: Rudder .......... full opposite to direction of rotation
Control wheel .......... as required to smoothly regain level flight attitude
checklist_verbatim.note: POH 3.3 SPIN RECOVERY, verbatim from the rendered page. 3.25 amplifies in prose: 'If a spin is inadvertently entered, immediately move the throttle to idle and the ailerons to neutral. Full rudder should then be applied opposite to the direction of rotation followed by control wheel full forward. When the rotation stops, neutralize the rudder and ease back on the control wheel as required to smoothly regain a level flight attitude.' NOTE PIPER'S ORDER: throttle idle and ailerons neutral FIRST, then rudder, then elevator - and ease back smoothly to avoid a secondary stall or an overspeed.

value: If both upper and lower latches are open, the door will trail slightly open and airspeeds will be reduced slightly.
To close the door in flight: Slow airplane to 89 KIAS; Cabin vents .......... close; Storm window .......... open
If upper latch is open .......... latch
If side latch is open .......... pull on arm rest while moving latch handle to latched position
If both latches are open .......... latch side latch then top latch
open_door.note: POH 3.3 verbatim. See other_systems.doors.open_door_in_flight for the 3.27 amplified text.

conditions_POH_VERBATIM.value: Under certain moist atmospheric conditions at temperatures of -5 deg C to 20 deg C, it is possible for ice to form in the induction system, even in summer weather. This is due to the high air velocity through the carburetor venturi and absorption of heat from this air by vaporization of the fuel.
conditions_POH_VERBATIM.note: POH 3.29 verbatim. NOTE THE POH'S OWN TEMPERATURE BAND: -5 C to +20 C. That is a type-specific number and is better in the oral than the generic 'below 70 F' from the PHAK. Note it includes temperatures BELOW freezing.

use_of_heat_verbatim.value: To avoid this, carburetor preheat is provided to replace the heat lost by vaporization. Carburetor heat should be full on when carburetor ice is encountered. Adjust mixture for maximum smoothness.

first_indication.value: A drop in RPM, possibly accompanied by a slight loss of airspeed or altitude, and engine roughness
first_indication.note: POH 3.41 (ENGINE ROUGHNESS) verbatim: 'Engine roughness is usually due to carburetor icing which is indicated by a drop in RPM, and may be accompanied by a slight loss of airspeed or altitude.' AN RPM DROP, because the propeller is fixed pitch and there is no manifold pressure gauge on this airplane. 'If too much ice is allowed to accumulate, restoration of full power may not be possible; therefore, prompt action is required.'

what_happens_when_you_apply_heat.value: RPM will decrease slightly and roughness will increase. Wait for a decrease in engine roughness or an increase in RPM, indicating ice removal. If there is no change in approximately one minute, return the carburetor heat to OFF.
what_happens_when_you_apply_heat.note: POH 3.41 verbatim. THE EXPECTED SEQUENCE IS THE SCORING ANSWER - it gets worse before it gets better, and one minute is the POH's waiting time.

full_heat_only_NOTE_verbatim.value: Partial carburetor heat may be worse than no heat at all, since it may melt part of the ice which will refreeze in the intake system. Therefore when using carburetor heat always use full heat, and, when ice is removed, return the control to the full cold position.

value: If roughness continues after one min: Carburetor heat .......... OFF
Magneto switch .......... L then R then BOTH
If operation is satisfactory on either one, continue on that magneto at reduced power and full RICH mixture to first airport.
engine_roughness.note: POH 3.3 verbatim. 3.41 adds: 'The engine will run rough if the mixture is too rich or too lean'; the tank switch is 'to see if fuel contamination is the problem'; and 'If roughness persists, prepare for a precautionary landing at pilot's discretion.' THIS IS A GOOD SYSTEMS ANSWER because it walks through induction, fuel and ignition in order.

gear_up_landing.note: THERE IS NO GEAR-UP LANDING PROCEDURE AND THERE CANNOT BE ONE - the PA-28-161 has FIXED landing gear (POH 7.1 'single-engine, fixed gear monoplane'; 7.7 'The fixed-gear PA-28-161'). Section 3 contains no gear emergency of any kind. The forced-landing procedure is POWER OFF LANDING (3.13), recorded above. If the examiner asks about a gear-up landing he is either testing whether the candidate knows his own airplane or has moved on to a complex aircraft question.

ditching.note: NO DITCHING PROCEDURE IS PUBLISHED in VB-1180 Section 3. The section contents are: Engine Fire During Start, Engine Power Loss During Takeoff, Engine Power Loss In Flight, Power Off Landing, Fire In Flight, Loss Of Oil Pressure, Loss Of Fuel Pressure, High Oil Temperature, Electrical Failures, Electrical Overload, Spin Recovery, Open Door, Engine Roughness, Carburetor Icing. Nothing else.

warm_up.value: Throttle 800 to 1200 RPM for not more than two minutes
warm_up.note: POH Section 4 WARM-UP checklist 'Throttle .......... 800 to 1200 RPM' and 4.17: 'Warm-up the engine at 800 to 1200 RPM for not more than two minutes... as this practice may result in fouled spark plugs.' On start, 'When the engine is firing evenly, advance the throttle to 800 RPM.'

taxi_caution.value: Do not operate the engine at high RPM when running up or taxiing over ground containing loose stones, gravel or any loose material that may cause damage to the propeller blades.
taxi_caution.note: POH 4.17 verbatim, printed twice on the page.

value: Magnetos .......... max. drop 175 RPM / max. diff. 50 RPM
Engine is warm for takeoff when throttle can be opened without engine faltering.
checklist_verbatim.note: POH Section 4.3 GROUND CHECK, transcribed verbatim from the rendered page (PDF 61, printed 4-8).

magneto_check_rpm.note: POH 4.19 'The magnetos should be checked at 2000 RPM' and the GROUND CHECK list 'Throttle .......... 2000 RPM'. NOW A POH FIGURE - the earlier pass could only corroborate it from three operator checklists.

maximum_drop.note: POH 4.19 'Drop off on either magneto should not exceed 175 RPM' and the GROUND CHECK list.

maximum_difference.note: POH 4.19 'and the difference between the magnetos should not exceed 50 RPM' and the GROUND CHECK list.

maximum_time_on_one_magneto.note: POH 4.19 verbatim: 'Operation on one magneto should not exceed 10 seconds.' A POH limit most candidates have never read.

vacuum_check.note: POH 4.19 'Check the vacuum gauge; the indicator should read 4.8" - 5.1" Hg at 2000 RPM' and the GROUND CHECK list. 5.1, not 5.2.

carburetor_heat_check_POH_VERBATIM.value: Carburetor heat should also be checked prior to takeoff to be sure the control is operating properly and to clean any ice which may have formed during taxiing. Avoid prolonged ground operation with carburetor heat ON as the air is unfiltered.
carburetor_heat_check_POH_VERBATIM.note: POH 4.19 verbatim. TWO REASONS FOR THE CHECK (control works; clear any taxi ice) AND THE REASON NOT TO LINGER (unfiltered air). The POH does not specify an expected RPM drop for the carb heat check.

carb_heat_expected_drop.note: VB-1180 DOES NOT PUBLISH AN EXPECTED RPM DROP FOR THE CARBURETOR HEAT CHECK. The GROUND CHECK list just says 'check' and 4.19 gives no number. He should say he looks for a definite drop and a smooth return, and that the POH does not specify a figure, rather than quoting a number from a school checklist as if it were a POH value.

electric_fuel_pump_off_check_POH_VERBATI.value: The electric fuel pump should be turned OFF after starting or during warm-up to make sure that the engine driven pump is operating. Prior to takeoff the electric pump should be turned ON again to prevent loss of power during takeoff should the engine driven pump fail.
electric_fuel_pump_off_check_POH_VERBATI.note: POH 4.19, verbatim from the rendered page (PDF 72, printed 4-19). THIS IS THE 'WHY' BEHIND THE GROUND CHECK ITEM 'Electric fuel pump OFF / Fuel pressure check'.

warm_enough_for_takeoff.value: The engine is warm enough for takeoff when the throttle can be opened without the engine faltering
warm_enough_for_takeoff.note: POH 4.19 and the GROUND CHECK list. A functional test, not an oil temperature number - which is a better answer than guessing a temperature.

value: Empty seats .......... seat belts snugly fastened
before_takeoff_checklist_verbatim.note: POH Section 4.3 BEFORE TAKEOFF, verbatim from the rendered page (PDF 61). The OCR text layer drops the final 'Air conditioner .......... OFF' line; it is on the page. 4.21 NOTE: 'The mixture should be set FULL RICH, but a minimum amount of leaning is permitted for smooth engine operation when taking off at high elevation.' Fuel selector 'proper tank (fullest)' per 4.21.
before_takeoff_checklist_verbatim.src: POH VB-1180 4.3 BEFORE TAKEOFF p.4-8 (PDF 61); 4.21 p.4-19 (PDF 72)

value: Control wheel .......... back pressure to rotate to climb attitude
normal.note: POH 4.3 TAKEOFF / NORMAL, verbatim. 4.23: 'The tab should be set slightly aft of neutral, with the exact setting determined by the loading of the airplane... Premature raising of the nose or raising it to an excessive angle will result in a delayed takeoff. After takeoff, let the airplane accelerate to the desired climb speed by lowering the nose slightly.' Takeoffs are normally made with flaps UP.

value.technique: Apply full power before brake release
value.obstacle_speed: accelerate to and maintain 44 to 57 KIAS (depending on weight) until obstacle clearance is achieved

short_field_no_obstacle_0_flaps.note: POH 4.3 '0 deg FLAPS TAKEOFF PERFORMANCE' and 4.23: 'A short field takeoff is accomplished without flaps by applying full power before brake release; lift off at 40-52 KIAS (depending on weight) and accelerate to and maintain 44-57 KIAS (depending on weight) past obstacle and climb out at 79 KIAS.' THE TRAP: the POH's plain short field takeoff is a NO-FLAP takeoff. The speed RANGES are weight-dependent and are quoted at and below 2440 lb, so at his lighter gross he is at the low end - but the ranges themselves may differ in VB-880.

value.technique: Apply full power before brake release
value.obstacle_speed: 44 to 57 KIAS (depending on weight) until obstacle clearance is attained
value.after_obstacle: accelerate to 79 KIAS and then slowly retract the flaps

short_field_with_obstacle_25_flaps.note: POH 4.3 '25 deg FLAPS TAKEOFF PERFORMANCE' and 4.23 verbatim.

value.technique: Accelerate and lift off nose gear as soon as possible. Lift off at lowest possible airspeed. Accelerate just above ground to 52 KIAS to climb past obstacle height.
value.then: Continue climbing while accelerating to best rate of climb speed, 79 KIAS. Flaps retract slowly.

soft_field_with_obstacle.note: POH 4.3 SOFT FIELD, OBSTACLE CLEARANCE and 4.23, verbatim. The 52 KIAS in-ground-effect acceleration target is a specific POH number.

value.technique: Accelerate and lift off nose gear as soon as possible. Lift off at lowest possible airspeed. Accelerate just above ground to best rate of climb speed, 79 KIAS.
value.then: Flaps retract slowly / retract the flaps while climbing out.

soft_field_no_obstacle.note: POH 4.3 SOFT FIELD, NO OBSTACLE and 4.23, verbatim.

why_flaps_for_soft_field.value: Takeoffs are normally made with flaps up; however, for short field takeoffs and for takeoffs under difficult conditions, such as deep grass or a soft surface, total distances can be reduced appreciably by lowering the flaps to 25 degrees and rotating at lower airspeed.

value: Electric fuel pump .......... OFF at desired altitude
climb.note: POH 4.3 CLIMB, verbatim. 4.25: 'The best rate of climb at gross weight will be obtained at 79 KIAS. The best angle of climb may be obtained at 63 KIAS. At lighter than gross weight these speeds are reduced somewhat.' ALL AT 2440 LB GROSS.

cruise.value: Normal max power 75%. Reduce to the desired cruise power setting and lean the mixture to peak RPM; adjust the throttle if necessary for final RPM setting.
cruise.note: POH 4.3 CRUISING 'Normal max power .......... 75%' and 'Reference performance charts and Avco-Lycoming Operators Manual.' 4.27 describes reducing to the cruise setting and leaning to peak engine RPM for 'best fuel economy'.

normal.value: Throttle set for 2500 RPM, mixture full rich, maintain an airspeed of 126 KIAS. In case carburetor ice is encountered apply full carburetor heat.
normal.note: POH 4.29 NORMAL verbatim: 'To achieve the performance on Figure 5-31, the power on descent must be used. The throttle should be set for 2500 RPM, mixture full rich and maintain an airspeed of 126 KIAS.' Note 126 KIAS is VNO - this is a descent right at the top of the green arc, so it is a smooth-air-only procedure.

power_off.value: If a prolonged power off descent is to be made, apply full carburetor heat prior to power reduction if icing conditions are suspected. Throttle should be retarded and mixture control leaned as required. Power response should be verified approximately every 30 seconds by partially opening and then closing the throttle (clearing the engine). When leveling off, enrichen mixture, set power as required and select carburetor heat off unless carburetor icing conditions are suspected.
power_off.note: POH 4.29 POWER OFF verbatim. CARB HEAT BEFORE THE POWER REDUCTION, NOT AFTER - and clear the engine every 30 seconds. Both are specific POH instructions and both are commonly got wrong.

checklist_verbatim.note: POH 4.3 LANDING checklist and 4.31, combined. The placarded LANDING CHECKLIST in 2.25 is the short version.

approach_speeds.note: POH 4.31 verbatim: 'The airplane should be trimmed to an initial-approach speed of about 70 KIAS with a final-approach speed of 63 KIAS with flaps extended to 40 deg. The flaps can be lowered at speeds up to 103 KIAS, if desired.' BOTH ARE 2440 LB SPEEDS.

mixture_and_carb_heat_POH_VERBATIM.value: The mixture control should be kept in full RICH position to insure maximum acceleration if it should be necessary to open the throttle again. Carburetor heat should not be applied unless there is an indication of carburetor icing, since the use of carburetor heat causes a reduction in power which may be critical in case of a go-around. Full throttle operation with carburetor heat on can cause detonation.
mixture_and_carb_heat_POH_VERBATIM.note: POH 4.31 verbatim. NOTE THIS CONTRADICTS THE COMMON HABIT OF CARB HEAT ON FOR EVERY APPROACH - Piper says do not apply it unless there is an indication of icing, because of the go-around penalty and the detonation risk at full throttle. A candidate who can quote this and explain the trade-off will stand out.

short_field_landing_technique.value: Normally, the best technique for short and slow landings is to use full flap and enough power to maintain the desired airspeed and approach flight path. Mixture should be full RICH, fuel on the fullest tank, and electric fuel pump ON. Reduce the speed during the flareout and contact the ground close to the stalling speed. After ground contact hold the nose wheel off as long as possible. As the airplane slows down, gently lower the nose and apply the brakes. Braking is most effective when flaps are raised and back pressure is applied to the control wheel, putting most of the aircraft weight on the main wheels.
short_field_landing_technique.note: POH 4.31 verbatim. A POWER-ON, FULL-FLAP, DRAGGED-IN SHORT FIELD APPROACH - which is what Piper publishes and what the commercial short field landing wants. Note the braking advice: flaps UP after touchdown.

crosswind_landing.value: In high wind conditions, particularly in strong crosswinds, it may be desirable to approach the ground at higher than normal speeds with partial or no flaps.

general_touchdown_guidance.value: The amount of flap used during landings and the speed of the aircraft at contact with the runway should be varied according to the landing surface and conditions of wind and airplane loading. It is generally good practice to contact the ground at the minimum possible safe speed consistent with existing conditions.

after_landing_and_shutdown.value: At the pilot's discretion, the flaps should be raised and the electric fuel pump turned OFF. The air conditioner and radios should be turned OFF, and the engine stopped by disengaging the mixture control lock and pulling the mixture control back to idle cut-off. The throttle should be left full aft to avoid engine vibration while stopping. Then the magneto and master switches must be turned OFF. NOTE: When alternate fuels are used, the engine should be run up to 1200 RPM for one minute prior to shutdown to clean out any unburned fuel.
after_landing_and_shutdown.note: POH 4.33 STOPPING ENGINE verbatim including the NOTE. The 1200 RPM one-minute burn-off before shutdown on alternate fuel is a detail almost nobody knows. The second NOTE repeats the flap-step warning.

parking.value: Secure the aileron and stabilator controls by looping the safety belt through the control wheel and pulling it snug. The flaps are locked when in the UP position and should be left retracted. Tie downs can be secured to rings provided under each wing and to the tail skid. The rudder is held in position by its connections to the nose wheel steering and normally does not have to be secured.
parking.note: POH 4.35 verbatim. THE RUDDER NEEDS NO EXTERNAL LOCK because it is connected to the nose wheel steering - a nice piece of system understanding.

stalls.value: The stall characteristics are conventional. An approaching stall is indicated by a stall warning horn which is activated between five and ten KTS above stall speed. Mild airframe buffeting and gentle pitching may also precede the stall. The gross weight stalling speed with power off and full flaps is 44 KIAS. With the flaps up this speed is increased. Loss of altitude during stalls varies from 100 to 275 feet, depending on configuration and power. NOTE: The stall warning system is inoperative with the master switch OFF.
stalls.note: POH 4.37 verbatim. The 44 KIAS and the 100-275 ft are 2440 lb figures.

value: COCKPIT: turn ON the master switch, check the fuel quantity gauges for adequate supply and check that the annunciator panel illuminates; turn OFF the master switch. Open the pitot and static drains.

RIGHT WING: open the fuel cap and visually check the fuel color, and the quantity should match the indication on the fuel quantity gauge; the fuel tank vent should be clear of obstructions; drain the fuel tank through the quick drain at the lower inboard rear corner.

NOSE SECTION: look for oil or fluid leakage; check the alternator belt for proper tension; check the engine baffle seals; check the oil level, make sure that the dipstick has been properly seated; open the fuel strainer on the left side of the fire wall long enough to remove any accumulation of water and sediment and check for proper fuel.

LEFT WING: fuel cap, fuel colour, quantity matches the gauge, vent clear, drain enough fuel to insure all water and sediment has been removed; remove the cover from the pitot/static head on the underside of the wing and make sure the holes are open and clear.
preflight_walkaround_fuel_and_oil_items.note: POH 4.13 PREFLIGHT CHECK, the fuel, oil and electrical items, transcribed from the rendered pages. Note the walk-around requires a VISUAL fuel check against the gauge on both wings, and the alternator belt tension check in the nose section.

oil_minimum_safe_quantity.note: POH 8.19 verbatim: 'The oil capacity of the engine is 8 quarts, and the minimum safe quantity is 2 quarts.' See oil.minimum_for_flight for the full discussion of why three other figures were circulating.

oil_change_interval.value: Every 50 hours, and sooner under unfavorable operating conditions

oil_filter_interval.value: Full flow cartridge type oil filters should be replaced each 50 hours of operation

oil_and_filter_calendar_limit.note: POH 8.19 'The interval between oil and oil filter change is not to exceed four (4) months.'

oil_grade_by_ambient_temperature.note: POH 8.19 table, transcribed cell by cell from the rendered page (PDF 169). The 'All Temperatures' row has a dash in the MIL-L-6082B column - no single-grade mineral oil is recommended for all temperatures. 'When operating temperatures overlap indicated ranges, use the lighter grade oil.' NOTE on the same page: 'Refer to the latest issue of Lycoming Service Instruction 1014 (Lubricating Oil Recommendations) for further information.' FOR A LATE-NOVEMBER CHECKRIDE the relevant rows are 0 to 70 deg F (SAE 30 straight, or 30/40/20W-40 ashless dispersant) and the all-temperature multigrades 15W-50 or 20W-50. CAUTION: Section 1.9(c) prints a SHORTER and slightly DIFFERENT table headed 'Oil Viscosity per Average Ambient Temp. for Starting' - Single: above 60 F SAE 50, 30-90 F SAE 40, 0-70 F SAE 30, below 10 F SAE 20; Multi: 40 or 50, 40, 40 or 20W-30, 20W-30. The two tables disagree in places (1.9 has no all-temperature row and gives 20W-30 below 10 F against 8.19's '30 or 20W-30'). Section 8.19 is the servicing table and is the one to quote.

oil_break_in.note: VB-1180 SAYS NOTHING ABOUT BREAK-IN OIL. Section 8.19 refers the pilot to Lycoming SI 1014. Lycoming SI 1014 requires non-dispersant mineral oil for the first 50 hours and after cylinder replacement until oil consumption stabilises, for engines other than the O-320-H and O/LO-360-E series - so it does apply to this D-series engine. Attribute that to Lycoming, not to the POH.

fuel_grade.value: Minimum aviation grade 100; 100 or 100LL Aviation Grade; AVGAS ONLY
fuel_grade.note: POH 8.21(b) 'The minimum aviation grade fuel for the PA-28-161 is 100. Since the use of lower grades can cause serious engine damage in a short period of time, the engine warranty is invalidated by the use of lower octanes.' POH 2.7(g) and the filler-cap placard: '100 or 100LL Aviation Grade'. POH 1.7(c)(1): '100 Green or 100LL Blue Aviation Grade'.

fuel_screens.value: At every 50-hour inspection, the fuel screens in the strainer, in the electric fuel pump, and at the carburetor inlet must be cleaned.

fuel_draining.note: Full procedure recorded under fuel.drains. Sumps first, then the strainer twice - once with the selector on each tank.

tire_pressures.note: POH 8.23 verbatim: 'For maximum service from the tires, keep them inflated to the proper pressures - 30 psi for the nose gear and 24 psi for the main gear.' Agrees with 7.7. 8.23 adds: 'All wheels and tires are balanced before original installation, and the relationship of tire, tube and wheel should be maintained upon reinstallation. Unbalanced wheels can cause extreme vibration in the landing gear... When checking tire pressure, examine the tires for wear, cuts, bruises, and slippage.'

value.nose_gear: 3.25 inches +/- .25 of strut exposure under normal static load
value.main_gear: 4.50 inches +/- .25 of strut exposure under normal static load

strut_servicing.note: POH 7.7 gives the nominal figures; POH 4.13 walk-around gives the tolerances.

battery_service_verbatim.value: Access to the 12-volt battery is obtained by raising upper right cowl and removing the cover of the battery box, which is mounted on the forward right face of the fire wall. The battery box has a drain tube which is normally closed off with a cap and which should be opened occasionally to drain off any accumulation of liquid. The battery should be checked for proper fluid level. DO NOT fill the battery above the baffle plates. DO NOT fill the battery with acid - use only water. A hydrometer check will determine the percent of charge in the battery. If the battery is not up to charge, recharge starting at a 4 amp rate and finishing with a 2 amp rate. Quick charges are not recommended.
battery_service_verbatim.note: POH 8.25, verbatim from the rendered pages (PDF 172-173). THE ACCESS LOCATION IS THE VB-1180 FIREWALL INSTALLATION AND MAY NOT BE HIS - see electrical.battery_location_FOR_HIS_SERIAL. The servicing instructions themselves (water not acid, do not fill above the baffle plates, hydrometer, 4 amp then 2 amp, no quick charges) are battery practice and carry across.

engine_air_filter.value: Wet-type polyurethane foam, in the lower right front of the engine compartment behind four quarter-turn fasteners, disposable, inspected at least once every 50 hours and more frequently in dusty conditions
engine_air_filter.note: POH 8.11 verbatim in substance. 'If it is excessively dirty or shows any damage' it is replaced, not cleaned - it is disposable.

propeller_service.value: The spinner and backing plate should be frequently cleaned and inspected for cracks. Before each flight the propeller should be inspected for nicks, scratches, and corrosion. If found, they should be repaired as soon as possible by a rated mechanic, since a nick or scratch causes an area of increased stress which can lead to serious cracks or the loss of a propeller tip.
propeller_service.note: POH 8.17 verbatim. 'The back face of the blades should be painted when necessary with flat black paint to retard glare.'

value: Before cleaning the engine compartment, place a strip of tape on the magneto vents to prevent any solvent from entering these units.
Do not spray solvent into the alternator, vacuum pump, starter, or air intakes.
Do not operate the engine until excess solvent has evaporated or otherwise been removed.

examiner_focus_notes: THE HANDBOOK MISMATCH IS STILL THE BIGGEST RISK. Everything in this file came from Piper Report VB-1180, which covers serials 28-8316001 and up. N84054 is 28-8116257 and is covered by VB-880. The SYSTEMS (Section 7) are the same airframe and he can quote them with confidence. THE WEIGHTS AND THE SPEEDS THAT DEPEND ON WEIGHT ARE NOT HIS. If he quotes 2440 lb gross or Va 111 KIAS and the examiner knows the serial blocks, everything else he says gets re-examined. The single best move before the ride: open the actual book in N84054 and photograph Section 2.

OIL MINIMUM FOR FLIGHT IS 2 QUARTS, AND IT IS IN THE POH. Section 8.19, first sentence: 'The oil capacity of the engine is 8 quarts, and the minimum safe quantity is 2 quarts.' The three figures that were in conflict are now resolved: 2 quarts is the POH MINIMUM SAFE QUANTITY; 6 quarts is the TCDS USABLE OIL figure, which is a weight-and-balance number; 6 to 8 quarts is one school's dispatch policy. Being able to name all three and say which is which is a much better answer than any one of them alone. He should still fly to his school's minimum, not to 2 quarts.

THE AMMETER IS A LOADMETER AND THE SENTENCE IS NOW IN HIS OWN MODEL'S BOOK. POH 7.15: 'Unlike previous generator systems, the ammeter as installed does not show battery discharge; rather, it indicates the electrical load on the alternator in amperes.' Alternator failure therefore shows as ZERO on the ammeter, not as a negative deflection - POH 3.23 says so explicitly. If he answers 'it shows whether the battery is charging or discharging' he has described a Cessna. Bonus detail straight from 7.15: night flight with radios is about 30 amperes, plus about 2 amperes for a fully charged battery.

THE ELECTRIC FUEL PUMP SENTENCE: 'The electric pump should be ON for all takeoffs and landings and when switching tanks.' (POH 7.13). And he should have the WHY from 4.19: it goes OFF during warm-up 'to make sure that the engine driven pump is operating', and back ON before takeoff 'to prevent loss of power during takeoff should the engine driven pump fail'. The pump is a BACKUP, not the normal supply. THE TRAP: both engine fire checklists turn the electric pump OFF with the fuel selector OFF - the opposite of every other fuel emergency.

BATTERY LOCATION IS A GENUINE TRAP THIS TIME. VB-1180 says the battery is 'in a box, mounted on the forward right face of the fire wall' (7.15 and 8.25). The VB-880 excerpt for his serial block says it is 'in a thermoplastic box immediately aft of the main spar'. Piper moved it. The widely circulated online POH will give him the wrong answer. HE MUST LOOK. If it is aft of the spar it is a weight-and-balance item behind the CG and unreachable in flight; if it is on the firewall it is in the engine compartment under the right cowl.

ENGINE DASH NUMBER. POH 1.3(c) and 2.7(c) both print 'O-320-D2A or O-320-D3G', exactly as the TCDS approves both, and the FAA registry records only '0-320 SERIES'. The right answer is 'both are approved for this model, and mine is the ___, which I read off the data plate'. His instructor's claim that the TCDS names the D3G is only half right.

CARBURETOR ICING TEMPERATURE BAND - USE THE POH'S OWN NUMBERS. POH 3.29: 'Under certain moist atmospheric conditions at temperatures of -5 deg C to 20 deg C, it is possible for ice to form in the induction system, even in summer weather.' That is a type-specific band and it beats the generic 'below 70 F' from the PHAK. First indication is an RPM DROP (3.41) because the propeller is fixed pitch and there is no manifold pressure gauge. Applying heat makes it WORSE first - 'RPM will decrease slightly and roughness will increase' - then better; wait about one minute.

CARB HEAT: FULL ON OR FULL OFF, AND THE AIR IS UNFILTERED - BOTH NOW POH-SOURCED. 3.41 NOTE: 'Partial carburetor heat may be worse than no heat at all, since it may melt part of the ice which will refreeze in the intake system.' 4.19: 'Avoid prolonged ground operation with carburetor heat ON as the air is unfiltered.' And the heat source is now nailed down: 7.5 says the heated air comes from a heater shroud on the muffler, the same shrouds that feed cabin heat and defrost.

CARB HEAT ON APPROACH - PIPER DISAGREES WITH THE COMMON HABIT. POH 4.31: 'Carburetor heat should not be applied unless there is an indication of carburetor icing, since the use of carburetor heat causes a reduction in power which may be critical in case of a go-around. Full throttle operation with carburetor heat on can cause detonation.' But for a PROLONGED POWER-OFF descent, 4.29 says apply full carb heat BEFORE the power reduction and clear the engine every 30 seconds. Knowing the difference between those two situations is a strong answer.

THE SHORT FIELD TAKEOFF TRAP. POH 4.23: 'A short field takeoff is accomplished WITHOUT FLAPS by applying full power before brake release.' It is the short field WITH AN OBSTACLE, and both soft field cases, that use 25 degrees (second notch). Most candidates say 25 degrees for every short field. The soft-field-with-obstacle number to remember: accelerate just above the ground to 52 KIAS to climb past the obstacle, then 79 KIAS.

RUN-UP NUMBERS ARE NOW POH NUMBERS, NOT CHECKLIST FOLKLORE. 2000 RPM; max drop 175 RPM; max difference 50 RPM; AND 'Operation on one magneto should not exceed 10 seconds' (4.19), which almost nobody quotes. Vacuum is 4.8 to 5.1 in Hg AT 2000 RPM - note 5.1, not 5.2. The POH publishes NO expected RPM drop for the carburetor heat check; he should say so rather than quoting a school figure as a POH value.

NO BOTH ON THE FUEL SELECTOR - and the Figure 7-7 selector face in the book is placarded L TANK 24 GAL / R TANK 24 GAL / FUEL OFF. He must also know the detent button that has to be held to reach OFF and that it releases automatically going back to ON, and that the pump goes ON when switching tanks. The 17-GALLON TAB (7.13: 'Usable capacity to the bottom of the indicator tab is 17 gallons') matters more on his 2325 lb airplane than on a 2440 lb one.

THREE FUEL DRAINS, AND THE SEQUENCE IS THE SCORING DETAIL. One quick drain per tank at the lower inboard rear corner, plus the strainer quick drain on the front lower corner of the firewall. POH 8.21(d): 'Each of the fuel tank sumps should be drained first. Then the fuel strainer should be drained twice, once with the fuel selector valve on each tank.' Most candidates drain the strainer once. The POH's word is STRAINER, not gascolator.

THERE ARE NO FUSELAGE STATIC PORTS. POH 7.21: 'Pitot and static pressure are picked up by a pitot head installed on the bottom of the left wing.' One combined pitot/static head. The static WICKS on the wings are precipitation-static dischargers and have nothing to do with it. The alternate static source is OPTIONAL, with the valve below the left side of the instrument panel - he must check whether N84054 has one. If it does, the operating conditions are the detail: storm window and cabin vents CLOSED, cabin heater and defroster ON, altimeter error less than 50 feet.

THE ANTI-SERVO TAB, IN PIPER'S OWN WORDS. POH 7.3: 'The stabilator incorporates an anti-servo tab which improves longitudinal stability and provides longitudinal trim. This tab moves in the same direction as the stabilator, but with increased travel.' Same direction (a balance or servo tab moves opposite); increased travel; and 7.9 adds it serves 'the dual function of providing trim control and pitch control forces'. He can prove it on the walk-around by pushing the stabilator trailing edge down and showing the tab following.

THE VACUUM FAILURE DIAGNOSTIC IS IN THE BOOK AND IT IS A COMPLETE ANSWER. POH 7.17: a gradual decrease 'may indicate a dirty filter, dirty screens, possibly a sticky vacuum regulator or leak in the system'; ZERO pressure 'would indicate a sheared pump drive, defective pump, possibly a defective gauge or collapsed line'. Dry pump, engine driven, shear drive - so it survives an alternator failure. And 7.17 warns that low readings above 12,000 ft and at low RPM 'on approach or during training maneuvers' are NORMAL, which matters during the checkride itself.

WHAT SURVIVES AN ALTERNATOR FAILURE, STRUCTURED. KEEP: the engine (magnetos are self-exciting), the vacuum gyros (engine-driven pump), the flaps (manual cable and handle), the brakes (hydraulic). LOSE as the battery drains: electric fuel pump, stall warning horn (4.37 NOTE: 'The stall warning system is inoperative with the master switch OFF'), fuel gauges, ammeter, annunciator, lights, radios, transponder, and the turn indicator, which 7.19 says is the ELECTRIC one. NO BATTERY ENDURANCE FIGURE IS PUBLISHED - do not quote minutes.

THE SPLIT MASTER EARNS ITS KEEP IN THE OVERLOAD PROCEDURE. ELECTRICAL FAILURES cycles ALT off, sheds load, checks and resets the ALT breaker, then ALT on, with BAT staying on throughout. ELECTRICAL OVERLOAD (alternator more than 20 amps above known load) does the opposite: ALT switch ON, BATT switch OFF. You cannot fly either checklist with a single-pole master. He should be able to justify the split switch purely from these two procedures.

THE FALSE ALT LIGHT. POH 7.15 NOTE, repeated at the head of the Section 3 ELECTRICAL FAILURES checklist: 'When operating with light electrical load and a fully charged battery, the Alternator Inop. light may illuminate due to minimal alternator output. If the alternator is functional a slight increase in electrical load should extinguish the Inop. indication.' So the first move on an ALT light is add a little load and watch. That is a POH-sourced answer that sounds like real airmanship because it is.

ANNUNCIATOR LIGHTS ARE A PROMPT, NOT A DIAGNOSIS. POH 7.15: they are 'provided only as a warning to the pilot that a system may not be operating properly, and that he should check and monitor the applicable system gauge to determine when or if any necessary action is required.' Three lights: alternator, low oil pressure, and low vacuum when the optional gyro system is installed.

STALL WARNING MARGIN IS A POH FIGURE NOW: 'The indicator activates at between five and ten knots above stall speed' (7.29, repeated in 4.37). And the stall warning is electrical - master off, no horn.

NO GEAR-UP PROCEDURE EXISTS AND HE SHOULD SAY SO CONFIDENTLY. The gear is fixed (7.1, 7.7). The forced landing procedure is POWER OFF LANDING: spiral over the field, 1000 ft above the field at the downwind position, 73 KIAS best gliding angle, slow to 63 KIAS when the field can easily be reached, touch down at the lowest possible airspeed with full flaps, and when committed shut off ignition, master, fuel selector and mixture and tighten the belts. There is also no ditching procedure in Section 3.

GLIDE: THE POH GIVES A SPEED, NOT A RATIO. 73 KIAS at 2440 lb, prop windmilling, flaps 0, no wind (Figure 5-33). No glide ratio is printed anywhere. The chart's own worked example is 3000 ft of altitude for 5.6 nautical miles, which is about 11.3:1 - but he should present that as reading the chart, not as a published number.

UTILITY CATEGORY IS WHERE THE COMMERCIAL MANOEUVRES LIVE, AND THE ENTRY SPEED IS THE WEIGHT TRAP. POH 2.15(b) approves steep turns, lazy eights and chandelles for bank angles exceeding 60 degrees, all at 111 KIAS - which is Va at 2440 lb. HIS entry speed will be lower. Utility also means NO aft passengers and NO baggage, positive limit 4.4 G instead of 3.8 G, and spins still prohibited. The POH publishes no separate flaps-up/flaps-down load factors - do not offer 2.0 G as a POH figure.

A DETAIL THAT SHOWS HE READ THE BOOK: POH 1.15 BAGGAGE SPACE prints '(b) Maximum Ramp Weight (lbs) 22' and '(c) Maximum Landing Weight (lbs) 20'. Those labels are a typesetting error copied from 1.11; 22 and 20 are the baggage door dimensions, as 7.27 confirms with 'a large 20 x 22 inch outside baggage door'. Spotting a known error in the handbook is worth more than reciting ten numbers.

NOVEMBER-SPECIFIC: the oil cooler winterization plate. POH 7.5 mentions it and the Section 2.25 placard says 'OIL COOLER WINTERIZATION PLATE TO BE REMOVED WHEN AMBIENT TEMPERATURE EXCEEDS 50 deg F.' He should look for it on the preflight and know the rule. Oil grade for a cold-morning ride: the 0 to 70 deg F row gives SAE 30 straight or 30, 40 or 20W-40 ashless dispersant, and 15W-50 or 20W-50 covers all temperatures.

GAPS HE SHOULD ADMIT RATHER THAN GUESS, because VB-1180 genuinely does not cover them: the thermostatic bypass/vernatherm arrangement in the oil system; the crankcase breather; the magneto drive in words; which plugs each magneto fires and how many there are; the battery amp-hour rating; the carburetor make and model; the expected carb heat RPM drop; and whether the nose gear steering arc is 30 or 20 degrees. 'That's not in Section 7 - I'd take it from the engine manual' is a stronger answer than a confident wrong one.
serial_caveats: MAXIMUM TAKEOFF WEIGHT, NORMAL CATEGORY. VB-1180 2.11(a) and 1.11(a) print 2440 LBS. NOT HIS. FAA TCDS 2A13 item XVI-A (serials 28-7716001 through 28-8216300) gives 2325 lb normal. USE 2325 LB. The utility figure, 2020 lb, is the same in both.

MAXIMUM RAMP WEIGHT. VB-1180 prints 2447 lb normal / 2027 lb utility, i.e. gross plus the 7 lb start/taxi/run-up fuel allowance. The 2447 figure is not his. The TCDS does not publish a ramp weight, so his must come from VB-880 Section 2.11. Do not compute 2332 and present it as a limit.
MAXIMUM LANDING WEIGHT. VB-1180 1.11(c) prints 2440 lb normal, the same as takeoff weight. His will be 2325 lb if VB-880 follows the same convention, but that is an assumption - confirm it.

DESIGN MANEUVERING SPEED. VB-1180 2.3 gives Va = 111 KIAS at 2440 lb and 88 KIAS at 1531 lb. HIS 2440 LB NUMBER DOES NOT EXIST. Interpolating the handbook's own line (which 2.3 expressly permits) gives about 108 KIAS at 2325 lb, and the sqrt(W) rule agrees - but the number he should quote is whatever VB-880 prints at his gross weight. The same applies to the 'Turbulent Air Operating Speed 111 KIAS' in 4.5(c), which is the same speed under another name.

THE VA PLACARD. The in-view-of-pilot placard in VB-1180 reads 'Va = 111 KIAS AT 2440# (SEE P.O.H.)'. The placard physically in N84054 will name a different weight and a different speed. He should read his own placard and quote that.

UTILITY CATEGORY MANEUVER ENTRY SPEEDS. VB-1180 2.15(b) and the UTILITY CATEGORY OPERATION ONLY placard give 111 KIAS for steep turns, lazy eights and chandelles - again Va at 2440 lb. The three approved manoeuvres carry across; the entry speed does not. This matters directly to the commercial flight test.

THE CG ENVELOPE. VB-1180 2.13(a) gives the normal-category forward limit as 88.3 in at 2440 lb and 83.0 in at 1950 lb and less, with straight-line variation. THE 2440 LB END POINT IS NOT HIS, so the whole upper part of his envelope is different - at 2325 lb the forward limit on the VB-1180 line would be about 87.2 in, but his envelope may simply stop at a different place. Section 6 Figure 6-15 is captioned '2440 MAX. GROSS WT.' and is not his envelope. The 1950-and-less points and the utility rows (2020 lb: 83.8 / 93.0) are at weights he can actually be at and are probably identical, but must be confirmed. The datum definition (78.4 in ahead of the wing leading edge at the inboard intersection of the straight and tapered section) and the loading arms (front 80.5, rear 118.1, fuel 95.0, baggage 142.8) are geometry and do carry across.

ALL OF SECTION 5 PERFORMANCE. Every chart - takeoff ground roll and distance, climb, cruise, landing distance, glide (Figure 5-33, 'WEIGHT 2440 LBS'), and the stall speed chart (Figure 5-5, whose weight axis is drawn to 'MAXIMUM WEIGHT - 2440 LBS') - is computed for a 2440 lb airframe. He must plan from VB-880's charts, not these. Note that the Figure 5-5 stall chart and some takeoff charts read down to lighter weights, so entering them at 2325 lb is not nonsense - but the certified maximum-weight line is wrong and the charts are not approved for his airplane.

STALL SPEEDS AND THE AIRSPEED INDICATOR ARCS. VSO 44 KIAS (bottom of the white arc, and 4.37 'The gross weight stalling speed with power off and full flaps is 44 KIAS') and VS1 50 KIAS (bottom of the green arc) are 2440 lb figures. At 2325 lb his airplane stalls slower. WHETHER THE ARCS PAINTED ON HIS INSTRUMENT ARE THE SAME IS A SEPARATE QUESTION - VB-880 specifies his markings and they may start lower. He should read the arcs off the actual instrument and compare them with his own book.
BEST GLIDE 73 KIAS. A 2440 lb speed (Figure 5-33 states the chart weight). His best glide speed is lower. The glide CHART is also not his.

VY 79 KIAS AND VX 63 KIAS. POH 4.25 says these are 'at gross weight' and adds 'At lighter than gross weight these speeds are reduced somewhat'. Gross weight means 2440 lb in this book. VB-880 will publish its own.

FINAL APPROACH 63 KIAS AND INITIAL APPROACH 70 KIAS. Section 4.5 states the Section 4 speeds are 'for standard airplanes flown at gross weight under standard conditions at sea level' - 2440 lb again. Also the takeoff rotation band (45-55 KIAS), the lift-off bands (40-52 KIAS), the obstacle-climb bands (44-57 KIAS) and the soft-field 52 KIAS.

BATTERY LOCATION - A REAL AIRFRAME DIFFERENCE, NOT JUST A NUMBER. VB-1180 7.15 and 8.25: 'in a box, mounted on the forward right face of the fire wall'. VB-880 7.15 (the NTSB docket copy for his serial block): 'mounted in a thermoplastic box immediately aft of the main spar'. Piper relocated the battery between the two serial blocks. The Section 8.25 battery access instructions in VB-1180 ('raising upper right cowl') therefore do not describe his airplane either. HE MUST OPEN N84054 AND LOOK.
NOISE LEVEL 72.9 dB(A) (2.23). Measured per FAR 36 on a 2440 lb airframe; his placarded noise level may differ.
WING LOADING 14.4 lb/sq ft AND POWER LOADING 15.3 lb/hp (1.17). Both computed at 2440 lb. At 2325 lb they would be about 13.7 and 14.5 - derived, not published.

THE FUEL FILLER PLACARD VARIANT. VB-1180 2.25 prints a graphic 'AVGAS ONLY / GRADE 100LL / GRADE 100' placard and explicitly restricts it to 'serial numbers 28-8316037 and up'. 28-8116257 gets the other one: 'FUEL - 100 OR 100LL AVIATION GRADE'. The handbook does his serial-block reasoning for him here, and saying so is a cheap way to show he understands applicability.

NOSE GEAR STEERING ARC. POH 7.7 says 30 degrees each side of center with the bungee fitted, and that 'Later aircraft have the bungee removed from the nose gear steering mechanism and are steerable through a 20 degree arc each side of center.' The handbook never defines 'later aircraft'. Unknown for a 1981 airframe - he should give both and say he would confirm.
REAR SEAT SHOULDER HARNESSES. POH 7.25: provided for the rear seats 'depending on the model year' as standard or optional. Unknown for 1981; look at the airplane.

ANYTHING MARKED OPTIONAL IN VB-1180 must be verified as fitted or not fitted on N84054 regardless of serial: the alternate static source, pitot heat, the vacuum system and gyros, the suction gauge, the VSI, the turn indicator, the primer, air conditioning, the ELT model (NARCO 10 vs 910), the carburetor ice detection system, Piper External Power, the overhead ventilating system and cabin blower, the oil cooler winterization plate, and locking fuel caps.

NOT A WEIGHT ISSUE BUT AN EDITION ISSUE: VB-1180 7.35 cites 'FAR 91.52' for the ELT. That is pre-1989 numbering; the rule is now 91.207. The handbook he quotes from has 1982 regulatory references throughout.

unverified.why: VB-1180's upper anchor is 88.3 in at 2440 lb, which is not his gross. His envelope above 1950 lb is unknown. The 1950-and-less and utility rows are probably identical but unconfirmed.

VB-1180 lists 'two magnetos' among the engine accessories but never states the drive arrangement in words.

The phrase 'impulse coupling' appears nowhere in VB-1180 (full text searched). Operating Tip 10.3(j) names the LEFT magneto for starting, and the Lycoming O-320-D3G parts catalog lists one plain and one impulse magneto. Combining the two is reasoning, not a POH statement.

unverified.why: VB-1180 says only 'a shielded ignition' and 'two magnetos'. No plug count and no harness assignment anywhere in the handbook.
The POH names the carburetor as a component but never gives a make, model or float type. The TCDS gives carburetor SETTINGS (10-5135 / 10-5009 / 10-5217) but not a part.

unverified.why: VB-1180 does not publish one. The GROUND CHECK list says only 'check' and 4.19 gives no number.
VB-1180 never uses the phrase 'wet sump'. It is correct for the O-320 family and is implied by the 8-quart engine oil capacity and the dipstick, but it is an engine fact, not a POH sentence.
Not described anywhere in VB-1180. Section 7.5 covers the cooler and winterization plate only; Section 8.19 covers quantity, interval and grade only. An engine-manual item.
No description of a crankcase breather or its routing anywhere in the handbook.

unverified.item: oil.filter_or_screen - which is actually fitted to N84054
unverified.why: VB-1180 8.19 names a full flow cartridge filter and does not describe a screen-only configuration, but it does not state categorically that every airframe has the filter. Confirm from the engine logbook and the accessory housing; it also determines whether Lycoming's 25-hour or 50-hour interval applies.
VB-1180 gives the voltage only; no amp-hour rating appears anywhere in the handbook. Read the battery label or the equipment list.

Inferred as flooded lead-acid from the 8.25 servicing instructions (water not acid, baffle plates, hydrometer). The handbook never names the chemistry, and a sealed/RG battery may have been fitted since.

DIRECT CONFLICT between VB-1180 (forward right face of the firewall) and the VB-880 excerpt for his serial block (thermoplastic box immediately aft of the main spar). Must be resolved by looking at the airplane.

7.19 describes an avionics bus fed through an optional radio master switch plus an emergency bus switch behind the lower right shin guard. No formal bus diagram is printed, and the radio master is optional, so the actual bus structure of N84054 is unconfirmed.

VB-1180 7.29 describes the audible alarm and the activation margin but not the detector mechanism or which wing it is on. The lift-detector-on-the-left-wing description comes from a Piper PA-28-family maintenance manual, not from this handbook.
Explicitly OPTIONAL in 7.21. Must be confirmed by looking below the left side of the instrument panel in N84054.
Section 7.17 is footnoted '*Optional equipment' and 7.19 lists the gyros and suction gauge as panel options. Required for IFR by 2.19(c). Confirm the installation.
7.7 gives both and defines the cutover only as 'Later aircraft'. Unknown for a 1981 airframe.
7.25 says they are standard or optional 'depending on the model year'. Unknown for 1981.
VB-1180 documents both a NARCO ELT 10 and a NARCO ELT 910 with different operating procedures. Which is installed, if any, is unknown.
No glide ratio is published. The ~11.3:1 figure is arithmetic off the Figure 5-33 worked example and is at 2440 lb.
The POH gives no design rationale. The mechanism (low wing, no gravity feed, engine-driven pump with electric backup, three-position selector) is sourced; the rationale is reasoning.

The 'only accurate at empty' claim is NOT in this POH - the full text was searched. It derives from the certification rule. The POH instead requires a visual cross-check against the gauge on every preflight.

Section 8.19 and Section 1.9(c) print two different oil viscosity tables that do not fully agree (1.9 has no all-temperature row and gives 20W-30 below 10 F against 8.19's '30 or 20W-30'). 8.19 is the servicing table and is recorded as authoritative, but the discrepancy is real and is in the handbook.
The TCDS certification basis paragraph was not fetched. POH 1.1 references C.A.R. 3 and FAR Part 21 Subpart J for the handbook's content, which is not the same statement.

Alternate static source, pitot heat, vacuum system and gyros, suction gauge, VSI, turn indicator, primer, air conditioning, ELT, carburetor ice detection, Piper External Power, overhead vents and cabin blower, oil cooler winterization plate, locking fuel caps. Each must be confirmed on the airplane and against its equipment list.
